Riendave, France (at the Spanish Frontier), July 9. ()—Spanish government militiamen halted a two-day retreat on the eastern front today and launched a series of counter-attacks against positions the insurgents had conquered including the fortified towns of Nules, 28 miles north of Valencia. Barcelona, July 9. (4—Insurgent warplanes raided the Barcelona area twice today, heavily bombing the workers’ quarters of the capital. Four planes descended on Badalona, a northern suburb occupied mainly by workers, during the morning and dropped nearly 50 bombs. This raid followed a moonlight attack on the northern outskirts of Barcelona. The number of victims was believed high, especially in Badalona, the target of repeated insurgent attacks which have killed more than 75 persons in the past two weeks.

MHANGHAT, July 8.—(AP)—Japanese military officials today demanded that the municipal council of the International Settlement “immediately undertake steps to prevent a recurrence” of anti-Japanese terrorism which resulted in the death of two of their nationals. The protest was delivered through the Japanese consul general and was the second to be lodged by Japanese following yesterday’s outbreak of shootings and bomb throwings as the Chinese-Japanese war entered its second year. Earlier the consul general expressed to the municipal council his dissatisfaction with the precautionary policing arrangements. More than 15 bombs were thrown in the series of guerrilla attacks within the settlement and two Chinese, besides the Japanese, were killed. 1938-05-05.text: (By United Press.) Paris, May 5.—Finance Minister Paul Marchandeau announced today that the franc would be held at a maximum rate of 179 to the pound sterling, in an effort—by agreement with the United States and Great Britain—to strengthen the currency and attract refugee French capital back to the country.

It was the Italian opinion that Mussolini sought to attain this goal without destroying the "Rome-Berlin Axis" — which, it is intimated, already has reached its zenith and is destined to lose its previous importance — or the good prospects of really friendly Italian relations with Britain and France. LONDON, May 5.—()—War Minister Leslie Hore-Belisha announced today he would raise an army of women as part of the British war machine he is rebuilding. Having set new records for recruiting men, the dynamic, shiny-cheeked minister said there was no reason why women should not serve in a modern army. He called a conference of women’s leaders at the war office tomorrow to discuss how women could be drilled to assist in time of war. There was no indication, however, that he planned to put women in the trenches.

WASHINGTON — The French-British-American monetary agreement emerged unshaken today from another French financial crisis. Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau Jr. said the tri-partite agreement would operate as usual to prevent speculation raids on the currencies of France, Great Britain and the United States. He said that the action of French Premier Edouard Daladier in setting a “floor” on the exchange value of the French franc is “within the spirit” of the pact. The treasury maintained telephonic communication with its representatives in Paris while the French government, ruling by dictatorial decree through special permission of parliament, stabilized the franc in relation to other currencies to defend it against speculative attacks. (Copyright, 1938, by United Press) London, England, May 5—(U P.)—Upon instructions of the state department American consulates in Europe are preparing and rechecking plans for evacuation to the United States of thousands of American residents in Europe in the event of war. The preparations include checking names and addresses of citizens entitled to American protection, a survey of various routes of evacuation, a survey of possibilities of transport including American-owned motor cars, and efforts to get Americans not now recorded at consulates to register their names and addresses. The preparations are designed to avoid the scenes of confusion of July and August, 1914, when thousands of panic-stricken tourists and residents rushed to unprepared consulates and were unable to obtain transportation or funds. DUBLIN, May 4—(AP)—The Irish government in a peace gesture on the election of Dr. Douglas Hyde as president today ordered the release of six prominent political prisoners. The release amounted to a general amnesty to Republicans since these six were the only ones in jail throughout the country. Mr. Hyde, a Protestant, was elected head of the predominantly Catholic state at a ceremony attended by representatives of all Ireland’s political parties. Invited by the state’s two largest parties to accept the presidency, Dr. Hyde was unopposed. Therefore, under the constitution, he was formally declared elected by acclamation for a seven-year term.

These informants, who were in a position to know what happened in the conferences between Mussolini and German Chancellor Adolf Hitler Wednesday, described Mussolini as ambitious to play the role of an “honest broker” in the current turbulent European political negotiations. To Keep Faith They believed he hopes to make good both his pledges to Hitler and to British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and observe scrupulously the terms of the newly-signed Anglo-Italian agreement as well as his earlier obligations to Germany. 1938-05-11.text: London, May 10—(P)—Seven Royal Air Force fliers were killed in three crashes today, a day after King George made flying visits to four air force stations. Five were killed in crashes of two planes belonging to the Wyton station, Huntingdonshire. Two others died when a plane from Helmsewell station, near Lincoln, fell.

GENEVA, May 11.—(#)—A cold reception awaited Ethiopia's titular king of kings today at Geneva where Great Britain and France drove their plans through the League of Nations council to make peace with his Italian conquerors. With the exiled Emperor Haile Selassie on his way from London to make a dramatic personal fight against the two powers who were this leading champions three years ago, his advisers fought for delay with complicated questions of procedure. Meanwhile Chile's ambassador to London, Augustin Edwards, warned the council that Chile might quit the League carrying other nations with her unless action was taken on her demands for covenant reform. Spain's delegate tonight halted the steamroller which Britain and France have been operating in the current session of the League of Nations council. Julio Alvarez del Vayo, Barcelona foreign minister, bitterly attacking the two powers for their bargaining with Italy, refused to let the question of intervention in the Spanish civil war be run through the council without full consideration. Maxim Litvinoff, Soviet Russia's foreign commissar, and William J. Jordan of New Zealand rushed to the defense of the Spaniard’s demand that the council take the question of intervention out of the hands of the 27-nation non-intervention committee in London. DUCKMANTON, Derbyshire, England, May 10—(4)—Two gas explosions killed 79 miners and injured more than 40 at the Markham coal mine here today. The disaster, which trapped an entire shift in the mine, struck into virtually every home in this little village. At first it had been feared a number of miners had been buried—alive or dead—but late tonight officials announced the whole pit had been examined and all men accounted for. Most of the bodies brought to the surface were so mutilated that it was virtually impossible to identify them. While rescue work was in progress, the bishop of Derby, Dr. A. E. J. Rawlinson, led hundreds of weeping women and bareheaded men in the Lord’s prayer at the pithead. The government started an investigation to determine the cause of the disaster, the worst since 265 were killed at Wrexham, Wales, Sept. 22, 1934.

DUCKMANTON, Derbyshire, England, May 31, P—The government began an investigation today to determine the cause of two gas explosions which killed 79 miners and injured more than 40 in the Markham coal mine yesterday.

SAN DIEGO, Cal., May 11—Friends of Col. Chas. A. Lindbergh said today he would end his voluntary exile in England and return to the United States only in the event his services were needed during wartime or some other national emergency. They said he had written of his plans to remain in England with his wife, the former Ann Morrow, and his sons, Jon and Land Morrow.

CHESTERFIELD, ENGLAND— (UP)— The death toll from a series of explosions in the Markham Colliery of the Stavely Coal and Iron Company was reported unofficially today to have reached 93. Seventy-nine were known dead in latest official reports, and more than 20 injured seriously. Fourteen others were missing and feared dead.

BOSTON, May 11.—(#)—The marriage of Miss Mary B. Dawes, young member of an old New England family, and Julian Denegal Steele, a Negro, former director of the Robert Gould Shaw house, a Boston philanthropic institution, was announced today at the office of Steele’s attorney. The announcement said the marriage ceremony had been performed recently in a small church in New York City with only a few intimate friends of the couple attending. Steele is a graduate of Harvard University.

Kennedy for removing thousands of Jews now suffering from violence and restrictive decrees in Germany. Prime Minister Chamberlain He said the problem had been taken up with governors of a number of British colonies and added that he hoped to make a statement on the whole question next week. The United States ambassador laid his proposals before Chamberlain Tuesday and the British government considered them in its meeting yesterday. The “Kennedy plan” has been described as calling for an effort to remove the majority of the 600,000 Jews now in Germany to North and South America and parts of the British, French and Netherlands empire. WASHINGTON, NOV. 17. (AP).—The greatest commercial accord of recent history, embracing a total American trade volume of $1,500,000,000 a year, was ready today for signature by high officials of the United States, Great Britain and Canada. Formal ceremonies for concluding the reciprocal agreements, apex of Secretary of State Hull's commercial program, were arranged for 4 p.m. Eastern Standard time in the famous east room of the White House. Embraced in the two new agreements are about 1,000 articles of export and import. Each treaty in printed form is the equivalent of a good-sized book. Products from all parts of the globe are involved in the agreements through inclusion of the British colonies. The importance of the trade with the colonies is indicated by the 1937 figures showing that the United States bought $322,560,000 worth of goods from them and sold them $76,897,000.

Washington, Nov. 16.—(#)—The United States and Great Britain drew closer together today by announcing the conclusion of their reciprocal trade agreement, while the United States and Germany drifted farther apart. The state department said the British and Canadian trade pacts would be signed at the White House tomorrow afternoon. Prime Minister Mackenzie King of Canada will come here for the signing. Secretary of State Hull, Mr. King and probably the British ambassador, Sir Ronald Lindsay, will speak after the ceremony. The Anglo-American agreement links two countries enjoying forty per cent. of the world’s trade, makes the 19th agreement concluded by Secretary Hull and brings within trade agreements about 60 per cent. of our total trade. LONDON — Great Britain and the United States neared agreement today on a plan to ransom German Jews and resettle them in what would be the most prodigious mass emigration in history. The plan, initiated by American Ambassador Joseph Kennedy and which would cost approximately $150,000,000, was expected to be submitted to a five-power directorate of the inter-governmental Jew committee. In its essence, the plan calls for Great Britain to provide land in her colonies, while Jewish and other private organizations of the United States raise money to finance their settlement. France and other colonial powers, as well as South American nations, might also be asked to contribute land. According to British sources, Ambassador Kennedy told Lord Halifax, British foreign minister, that the United States government would not be able to contribute money to the plan,

LONDON, Nov. 17.—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the House of Commons today that the government is treating the problem of settling Jewish refugees from Germany in the British Colonies as a matter of urgency. Chamberlain said he has taken up the question with several colonial governors, including the governors of Tanganyika, East Africa, and hoped to be able to make a statement next week. Chamberlain's promise of a statement was taken as an indication that Britain and the United States have reached an agreement on rescuing some 700,000 Jews from their plight in Germany, and that only details need to be worked out. The government canvassed many parts of the Empire for suitable settlement places. British Guiana was among those considered, provided sufficient funds can be raised in the United States and elsewhere to finance the development of that difficult country. About $150,000,0

Rome, Nov. 16.-(P)—Italy and Great Britain finally made effective today a seven-months-old pact, settling their quarrel arising out of the Ethiopian war. The Earl of Perth, British ambassador, and Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo Ciano signed a brief declaration making operative the Anglo-Italian agreement of April 16 which among other things recognized the Italian conquest of Ethiopia. The friction dates from November 17, 1935, when economic penalties, sponsored by Britain and France, with 50 League of Nations members, went into operation to isolate Italy in the 1935 African war. Italian sources, however, declared Italy was still welded "strongly and firmly and with a full consciousness of responsibilities" to Germany in the Rome-Berlin axis. BERLIN—United States commercial attache called home before January 1. PARIS—Hugh R. Wilson, United States Ambassador to Germany, stops en route to Washington to report to President Roosevelt. DUESSELDORF—Nazis give martyr’s funeral to German diplomat slain in Paris by Jew; Hitler attends, Von Ribbentrop speaks. LONDON—Britain sees new trade treaty with United States as boost to Anglo-American cooperation. RIO DE JANEIRO—Brazil’s foreign minister praises Roosevelt’s plan to defend the Americas. ZARAGOZA—Insurgent observers say Franco’s Ebro campaign has paved way to end resistance of Government Spain.

N.S, Staff Correspondent) LONDON, Nov. 17—(INS)—A Reuter dispatch from Vienna said today that former Austrian Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg probably will not be brought to trial, according to a statement by an official Nazi spokesman. The report added that it was “privately believed” that Schuschnigg may be released within a few months on condition that he remain in Germany. He has been in custody ever since the annexation of Austria by the Reich.

These sources asserted London and Paris had decided to—Czechoslovakia to make utmost concessions to her Nazi minority and to warn Germany against committing any ‘action of violence’ against the central European republic. The representations, it was said, will be made within the next 24 hours, while Hitler and Benito Mussolini are conferring in Rome during the Fuehrer’s state visit to Italy. Foreign office circles said the decision came after receipt of diplomatic dispatches from Rome, reporting that the Italian and German general staffs were studying a plan of action should France and Great Britain “react” after a German coup in Czechoslovak

PARIS, May 6.—(4)—A joint Franco-British appeal to Czechoslovakia to make utmost concessions to her Nazi minority and a warning to Germany against committing any "action of violence" on the Central European Republic will be made within the next 24 hours, sources close to the foreign office declared today. Representations by the two governments in an effort to wipe out a threat of European war will follow decisions made by the French and British ministers at their meeting in London a week ago to arrange a common front in defense and foreign policy. Sir Neville Henderson, British ambassador at Berlin, will see Field Marshal Hermann Wilhelm Göring, No. 2 Nazi and Acting Chancellor during Reichsfuehrer Hitler’s absence in Italy, today, it was said. The French and British ministers in Prague will call at the same time on the Czech foreign office.

National government of Neville Chamberlain lost another bye-election to the Labor party today despite the fact that cabinet ministers for the first time in six years were permitted to make speeches in support of the government candidate. C. C. Poole, 35-year-old railway clerk, was elected to the House of Commons from the Lighfield constituency, near Birmingham, over C. B. Craddock, government candidate, by a majority of 826. Poole said he was elected 'because the people have no faith in the foreign policy of the government.' 'No longer can Mr. Chamberlain say the people of Britain share his childlike faith in dictators,' he declared.

Paris, May 5.—Premier Edouard Daladier pulled France out of the immediate financial hole today by revaluing the French franc and pinning it to the British pound sterling. The government fixed a lower limit of 179 francs to the pound sterling as the new bottom—equivalent to 35.80 francs to the dollar at the rate of $5 to the pound. Devaluation—the third since the World War—will give paper profit of more than 31,208,000,000 francs on the Bank of France's gold reserves. This step may be delayed for technical reasons. The government, which Daladier earlier estimated would need 35,000,000,000 francs to carry through 1938, however, has an obligation of more than 40,000,000,000 francs to the Bank of France. The Aim— Finance Minister Paul Marchandeau announced the new monetary measure as 'an operation whose goal is to achieve, first, de facto stabilization.'

LONDON, (UP).—Sir Victor Christian William Cavendish, 69, ninth duke of Devonshire, one of the greatest noblemen of the British peerage, died today at his famous estate Chatsworth House in Derbyshire. The duke had served as governor general and commander-in-chief of Canada from 1916 to 1921, and as secretary of state for the colonies in the cabinet from 1922 to 1924.

London, May 6.—Chinese armies today made perhaps their greatest bid to smash the Japanese conquerors of North China. The Chinese communist army of Gen. Chu Teh, known as the "Red Napoleon," reportedly penetrated far into the Japanese-controlled north for an attack on Peiping—a climax of devastating guerilla fighting that has sapped Japanese military might. Gates of the ancient city, Japan's provisional capital for the area, were closed and artillery fire rattled the windows of Peiping houses. For to the south, where the Japanese front lines had spread too far, the opposing troops were locked in a battle for control of the Grand Canal trenches where the Japanese offensive was halted. The invaders were seeking to capture Suchow-Fu, key to the Lung-Hai railroad, by a series of encircling and flanking movements intended to find a weak spot in the Chinese lines. HOLLYWOOD—UP)—Lew Brice said goodbye to his $150,000 poker pot today, after offering to flip coins for it—‘double or nothing’—with Harry T. Clifton, the English squire. Brice, younger brother of Fanny Brice, stage and movie comedienne, gave Clifton his signed releases of any claim against the money. He also was reported to have handed over Clifton’s two checks, one for $50,000 and the other for $100,000. Brice won the money at poker a week ago. The wealthy English sportsman stopped his court action designed to prevent Brice from cashing the checks. He had contended that Brice falsely represented himself as able to pay if the game had ended with Clifton the winner. The peace settlement occurred in the offices of Clifton’s lawyer, Jerry Giesler, after Brice made one last gesture. “I’ll flip him for it,” Brice said. “Just a flip of the coin, winner take double or nothing. 1938-09-24.text: BUDAPEST, Sept. 24—(4)—The American legation in Budapest had a train ready today to evacuate United States citizens in an emergency. The British legation made similar preparations. The American train was ready to leave immediately for the coast. (Trieste, Italy on the Adriatic Sea is the nearest port.) The legation advised all American citizens in Hungary to leave immediately if they could manage to do so. The Hungarian-Czechoslovak border was closed. Czechoslovakia and Hungary rushed military preparations in the frontier area.

London, Sept. 24—(7);—Adolf Hitler’s terms for peaceful settlement of the central European crisis were stated in official Czechoslovak circles today to call for revision of Czechoslovakia’s frontiers without any German guarantee of the new borders unless Hungary and Poland also became guarantors. This was interpreted by observers as strongly implying Hitler's support for the demands of Poland and Hungary for return of their minorities in Czechoslovakia. Czechoslovaks said Hitler’s definite terms were: 1. German occupation before October 1 of all Sudeten areas where more than 75 per cent of the population is German; 2. Evacuation of all Czechoslovak soldiers and civil servants from these areas by the same date; 3. (By Associated Press) LONDON, Sept. 24.—Prime Minister Chamberlain told his ministers today of the frail foundation of Europe’s peace after his fateful visits with Reichsführer Hitler while Britain joined a Europe-wide rush to get ready for war. The prime minister apparently had only a virtual ultimatum for Czechoslovakia expiring October 1—a week from today—to show for his desperate midnight parley on the banks of the Rhine. Before he climbed from his plane at Heston, the British home fleet was steaming out of Invergordon, Scotland, for a strategic place in the North Sea in the event of war and other arms of Britain’s military services were making similar extensive preparations for any emergency. Key to Peace For anxious Britain, the prime minister had only these words: “My first duty now: that I have come back is to report to the British and French governments the result of my mission.

GODESBERG, Germany, Sept. 24. (U.P)—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain carrying with him the hope of all Europe, returned to London today to make what it seemed must be the final effort to avert a war. The British leader left his hotel on Peter’s Hill, at Koenigs-Winter across the Rhine from Godesberg where he had conferred with Adolf Hitler, at 2:43 a.m. (CST) to take an airplane to London. In his final conference with Hitler, which ended early this morning, Chamberlain had agreed to submit a new set of proposals to the Czechoslovak government, regarding the method of surrendering the Sudeten minority area to Germany. Chamberlain made the proposals direct to Prague, without waiting for approval by his own cabinet.

LONDON, Sept. 24 (Saturday).—(*) London in a few terrifying hours came to the edge of war last night, as peace talks between Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Adolf Hitler wavered, then ended in "final" German demands on Czechoslovakia. It was noted here that Chamberlain left the Godesberg conference, which earlier in the day had been threatened with deadlock, merely bearing the German fuehrer’s final word to the Prague government on the Sudeten crisis. There was no mention of British support for these demands. It was believed generally in London that Hitler was demanding immediate demobilization of the Czechoslovak army and occupation of Sudetenland by either Sudeten or German troops. zy Boston, Mass., Sept. 23.—Appalled by the horror and desolation left by New England’s first hurricane and tidal wave, thousands of rescue workers tonight fought flood waters and frantically dug deeper into areas which already estimated their dead at more than 400. With wrecked communication lines rendering impossible a complete evaluation of the destruction, the possibility existed that the New England death toll might rise to 500 or beyond. Rhode Island, the nation’s smallest state, was the hardest hit, with large areas all in darkness, and all but cut off from the outside. Unofficial sources put the death count at around 245, and declared it probably would rise more. Massachusetts stood next on the list, with an estimated death list of 120 and some still missing. Ruiff, of Chicago, a Sudeten German deputy in the Czechoslovak parliament named Wollner and an unnamed British journalist. Although Miss Freeman-Mitford was subjected to a thorough examination by Czechoslovak road patrols in the wee hours of the morning, the authorities denied reports she was suspected of espionage and said she was not arrested. (Oy 220 ASV 2a Gas} Akron, O., June 1—William Schoenbeck, 69-year-old farmer was hoeing potatoes today when he learned his ticket on Bois Roussell in the English derby had won $150,000. “Goodness sakes,” he cried, dropping his hoe. Schoenbeck walked to the farmhouse and sat in the sun. “I am going to celebrate by not doing any more hoeing today,” he said.

LONDON — An 80-mile-an-hour gale smashed small towns of Southern England. One yachtsman died of exposure and another was feared lost. Many were rescued by lifeboats and warships rushed to the aid of distressed yachts and fishing boats. The storm kept the liner Queen Mary outside the harbor of Cherbourg, France, for 16 hours before she could pick up New York-bound passengers there. It flattened every tent in an army camp of 800 soldiers at Manorbier, Wales, tore a balloon loose from its moorings and razed show tents at Bournemouth’s Swank Royal Counties Agricultural Show.

The American youth, William Mueff, 22, described as a residential student from Chicago, immediately appealed to the United States legation in Prague for aid in obtaining his release. Mueff and the 24-year-old English girl were among four persons seized. Miss Freeman-Mitford had been in difficulties before. The plan was said to call for: In Spain First, an attempt to bring the Spanish government and insurgents together in an armistice ending the 22-month civil war. Second, negotiations for solution of Czechoslovakia's difficulties with her restless Germanic minority which Adolf Hitler has pledged.

LONDON, June 2—Great Britain intends to work actively to arrange an armistice in the Spanish civil war in addition to seeking a pacific settlement of the Czechoslovak minority problem and eventual direct friendship negotiations with Germany, it was disclosed today. Unsatisfied with the relatively negative efforts of the Spanish non-intervention committee, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain intends to go beyond the scope of the committee's work and try to effect an agreement that would end the civil war which in nearly two years has cost Spain hundreds of thousands of lives and billions of dollars in money, and has remained a constant menace to the peace of all Europe. It was understood that the government might seek the collaboration of France and possibly Italy also to sound out the Spanish Nationalists and Loyalists on their attitude toward an armistice. 1938-06-20.text: HYDE PARK, N. Y., June 20 (4—Rested and in gay mood from a week-end cruise down the New England coast and up the Hudson river, President Roosevelt plunged today into a mass of work—mostly concerned with bills passed by congress in its closing days. The president called immediately for secretaries upon his return to his family home here. He said, at a brief informal press conference on the Poughkeepsie dock, that he would start immediately on the bills which require his signature within the next few days if they are to become law. Mr. Roosevelt declined to answer a question regarding discussion in Washington that a special session of congress might be called to consider railroad legislation.

Great Britain today intensified her struggle to break through a maze of diplomatic and military conflict barring the way to consolidation of Europe's peace. Although the Spanish Civil War and other facts provide the immediate problem, the major aim of the campaign directed by Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain is alleviation of war danger created by expansion of Nazi Germany against the weakened post-war political and economic structure. Chamberlain's route to the goal has been slow, roundabout and difficult. The war in Spain provides the immediate obstacle, not because German and Italian support for the rebels is a threat to Britain's power (Chamberlain has chosen to ignore that for the present) but because it is preventing inauguration of the new Anglo-Italian friendship treaty. P.)—Premier Benito Mussolini is considering a British suggestion that he will seek a truce in the Spanish Civil War as one means of speeding operation of the Anglo-Italian pact, it was confirmed in well-informed quarters today. Diplomatic circles reported that Lord Perth, British ambassador, made the suggestion to Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italian foreign minister. The latter was reported to have transmitted the proposal to Mussolini, who is now at Rocca delle Caminate. It was not known when Mussolini's decision would be communicated to Lord Perth.

WIMBLEDON, Eng, ()-Donald Budge of Oakland, Calif, holder of every major world tennis championship, opened the defense of his all-England title today with an easy victory over Kenneth Ganda Dower of England. The scores were 6-2, 6-3, 6-3. The big redhead, who was given the customary honor of playing the first match of the tournament on the center court, slapped the ball with majestic indifference and seldom left the baseline. Ganda-Dower’s soft lobbying game was pie for Don. Henner Henkel of Germany, another seeded star, opened with a 6-2, 6-0, 6-2 victory over D. M. Bull of England.

Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo Ciano and the Earl of Perth, Britain's ambassador, met at noon to consider such possibilities. 1938-12-22.text: Perth, Scotland, Dec. 22 (UP)— Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s policy of European appeasement won a victory today when W McNair Snaddon, official conservative party candidate, defeated the Duchess of Atholl, insurgent conservative, in the Kinross and Western division by-election. Article two empowers the government to levy 10,000,000,000 francs ($264,000,000) in additional taxes direct and indirect, envisaged in decrees passed by the government under the emergency powers it enjoyed during the recess of parliament last fall. The sum is needed to balance the 1939 budget. Snaddon, who supported the prime minister's foreign policy, polled 11,808 votes compared to 10,495 for the duchess, a bitter critic of the Chamberlain appeasement program and so vigorous a foe of dictators that she had been given the nickname of “Red Kitty.”

CRIEFF, Scotland, Dec. 22 UP - The duchess of Atholl, who rebelled against Prime Minister Chamberlain's foreign policy, was beaten by 1,313 votes in the parliamentary by-election she forced to test the issue, complete returns showed today. The "red duchess," so called because of her support of the Spanish government cause, in yesterday's voting received 10,495 votes to 11,808 for William McNair Snadden, her conservative opponent who campaigned as a hearty supporter of Chamberlain's policy of appeasement. The wealthy duchess ran as an independent after resigning her seat in the House of Commons, in which she had represented the Kinross and West Perth division for 15 years. Her conservative highland constituents turned against her after she had broken formally with the prime minister's party after his Munich accord with the dictators for the partition of Czechoslovakia.

The reports ranged from assertions that hundreds of persons had been arrested to one that 45 Italian soldiers had been waylaid and hanged by angry Spaniards. United Press correspondents placed at strategic centers of communication along the frontier agreed that there had been a series of incidents in Nationalist Spain but insisted that many reports were exaggerated. It was true, also, that there seemed suspicion among the Loyalists that the Nationalists themselves were not discouraging the disaffection reports, hoping that the Loyalists would relax their vigilance in Eastern Spain where the Nationalists for weeks had been planning a mass offensive. London, Dec. 21.—()—Prime Minister Chamberlain's government told worried British householders today it would give them millions of private backyard bomb shelters made of steel. This project for individual “mail order” air raid refuges is part of a general plan that will cost the government more than $100,000,000. It was announced today by Sir John Anderson, the new minister for civil defense and lord privy seal, before the House of Commons. It is attuned to the theory that every Englishman's home is his castle and it is unique in world annals of home defense. Air raid protection in private or public shelters is provided, in the whole project, for 20,000,000 persons, or about half of the United Kingdom's population. The backyard bomb shelters will protect 10,000,000 who live in small, non-basement houses. The shelters will come in pieces easily put together, something like the prefabricat

London, Dec. 21.—(4)—Iceland sweltered today as Europe's great freeze added a few more deaths to the several score reported this week. The temperature at Reykjavik, Iceland’s capital, usually below freezing in December, reached 45 degrees, permitting farmers to work their soil. Normally the ground is frozen from October to spring. The cold wave in Europe rolled in from Soviet Russia. The coldest point there yesterday was Novosibirsk, 54.4 below zero. Moscow reported five below today. The temperature there Sunday was 14.8 below.

HONGKONG. (UP). Generalissimo Chiang Kai-Shek has compelled the United States and Great Britain to face squarely the issue of maintenance of a free and independent China. In talks with British and American ambassadors the leader of China’s millions capitalized on a military and economic situation as tense in its way as anything Europe has produced to press his plea for aid from the world’s democracies. Credit for any such help in the form of British and American credits to China—where the Japanese conquest is closing the open door to trade—must go to Chiang. Would ‘Turn Elsewhere, In his talks with the ambassadors, reliable sources said, he made it plain that if China did not receive encouragement from the democracies she would turn elsewhere—either toward Soviet Russia or to the totalitarian states, possibly seeking easy peace terms through German mediation. The showdown between China a

Paris, Dec. 22. — Premier Daladier’s plan to reorganize French finances by decree received approval for the second time today by the slim majority of seven votes in the chamber of deputies. The chamber ratified by a vote of 289 to 284 the inclusion in the 1939 appropriation bill of a section carrying implied approval of all the decree laws issued under the new three-year economic plan. Daladier, who staked the life of his government on the vote, made little attempt to hide his opinion that the cabinet had barely squeezed out of a tight place, but declared he was optimistic over the formation of a “faithful majority” upon which he could depend. The new test of Daladier's strength, the second since parliament convened earlier this month, came unexpectedly when the premier demanded that the 1939 appropriation bill be passed unchanged. The opposition sought to cancel one of the government's

of force to achieve some striking success. - PARIS, Dec. 22, The foreign Italy considers the 1935 Mussolini-Laval convention concerning Tunisia "no longer valid." Officials declined to disclose the text of the Italian communication or to give any indication of what action the French government might take. The convention assures Italians in Tunisia their right to Italian citizenship until 1965. It also defines the borders between Tunisia and Italian Libya and the borders between Italian Eritrea and French Somaliland in East Africa. It never has been ratified by the French Parliament, but French diplomatic experts consider that it has been in force since it was signed at Rome Jan. 7, 1935. They contend, therefore, that any Italian demands concerning Tunisia or French Somaliland must be based on the treaty. (Both territories have been targets of recent Italian clamor for French possessions.

1938-05-08.text: LONDON,—-Britain and France edged into Adolf Hitler's “family affair” with Czechoslovakia Saturday in the shadow of the feast of the bargaining dictators in Rome. Diplomats of the two nations urged peaceful means on Germany and concessions up to the limit of Czechoslovakia to solve the latter republic's minority problem. In Praha, the British and French ministers informed Dr. Kamil Krofta, Czechoslovak foreign minister, of the points of view of their respective governments. In Berlin, British Ambassador Sir Neville Henderson called on Dr. Ernst Woermann, undersecretary of state, to inform him of the action the diplomats took in Praha. But Britain and France were not in a warning mood Saturday. They were not surprised at reports from Rome that Premier Benito Mussolini of Italy had promised the German fuehrer a free hand in the campaign for the 3,500,000 Germans in Czechoslovakia. Mussolin

LONDON, May 5—(Sunday)—(INS)—Russia’s anti-Stalin “will o' the wisp” radio today reported that 45 persons were executed May 3 in a plot against the Soviet dictator, the Sunday Express said today. The wireless station is said by the Express to move about in a van, defying efforts of the secret police to locate it. “Our comrades, who tried to kill the Georgian dog Stalin on May 1, were betrayed by treachery and shot May 3,” the ghost station was quoted by the Sunday Express as saying. “We will avenge them!” The Express said the plotters were members of a secret organization called the “liberators of Russia.”

| SHANGHAI, May 7—Three thousand Chinese guerilla troops, fighting recklessly in the streets, threatened today to annihilate the Japanese garrison of Nantungchow, a supply base on the Yangtze River, 60 miles north of Shanghai. Japanese reinforcements were rushed from Shanghai in a desperate effort to save the garrison and retain possession of the important point. The loss of the town would cut supply and communication lines serving a Japanese army of 10,000 men in north Kiangsu province. This army was last reported 60 miles north of the Lunghai railway, fighting in the vicinity of Founing. Foreigners arriving from Yangtze ports said scores of Chinese civilians had been killed while hand-to-hand fighting raged inside the walls of Nantungchow. The guerillas infiltrated Nantungchow and attacked by surprise, inflicting many casualties among the Japanese garrison, numbering 300 men at the out

ROME, May 7—(P)—Benito Mussolini and Adolf Hitler completed and sealed their alliance tonight in an exchange of fidelity toasts at a formal state dinner in Palazzo Venezia. The Fuehrer guaranteed “for all time” the Alpine border between Germany and Italy. Their blanket reaffirmations of the solidity of the Berlin-Rome working agreement was interpreted as an indication they had struck a bargain with respect to each other's interests, wherever they meet, and would give each other mutual aid in the remaking of Europe. Hitler spent two hours in conversations with Italian leaders preparatory to tonight's speeches. After talking in private for an hour, Hitler and Mussolini called in their foreign ministers, Joachim Von Ribbentrop and Count Galeazzo Ciano, and the conversations continued for another hour. The chief topic was reported to have been a possible four-power pact involving France, Gre

SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain, May 7. (*)—Spanish insurgents, advancing down the coast toward Castellon de La Plana, inflicted heavy losses on government forces today in a drive that routed them from mountain positions at bayonet point. Insurgent military reports said the government troops had attempted to infiltrate behind the insurgent lines but were driven back. Heavy rains and wind storms still prevented operations on a large scale.

SHANGHAI — (®)—Chinese guerrilla armies struck Sunday in apparent coordination to break Japan’s hold in North China. Chinese sources asserted fully 13,000 irregulars were concentrated at Peiping, Japanese-held North China city, and had the moral support of the population. Savage fighting continued at Nantungchow, on the north shore of the Yangtze river 60 miles north of Shanghai, an important supply base for a Japanese army of 10,000 striking north through Kiangsu province toward the Lunghai railroad. A Japanese garrison of 300 there was said to face annihilation by 3,000 Chinese guerrilla troops which caught the Japanese unaware. Chinese said units of their 68th army had penetrated into southeastern Hopeh province after smashing Japanese lines north of Tsinan, the Japanese-held Shantung province capital. Japanese war planes operated over a wide area in attempts to break openings for the

SHANGHAI, Sunday, May 8— Chinese Communists today attacked Lukouchiao, in Peiping’s southwestern suburbs, where the Chinese-Japanese war started exactly 10 months ago. The war began last July 8 with an “incident” at Lukouchiao when the Japanese charged the Chinese garrison with an “unwarranted attack.” Today, Gen. Chu Teh, the “Red Napoleon” of the Far East, was determined to avenge the incident. Chu Teh's warriors attacked from three sides, the west, south and east. The Japanese met them and claimed to have repulsed all attacks. But the Japanese commanders feared that Chinese inside their lines, forced to bow to the invaders for 10 months, might rise up if arms simultaneously with a fresh attack from the outside. Chinese authorities in Hankow, the provisional capital, openly admitted that the Communists, now recognized as the 8th Route Army, were attacking today because this was the 10-

Hendaye, France (at the Spanish Frontier), May 7.—(#)—Spanish Insurgents tore a gap through government defenses in eastern Spain today and advanced five miles nearer the “lifeline” highway link between Madrid and the Mediterranean ports of Castellon de la Plana and Valencia. Insurgent commanders reported the government line was broken 40 miles north of Castellon where they captured the town of Portell, deep in the pocket protecting the government's central coast lines. Co-ordinated with this movement was a drive directly south of insurgent coastal columns, Valencia and Castellon were the object of both operations. The double thrust to broaden the insurgent foothold on the eastern coast and close two gateways for supplies into the larger of the two segments of government territory broke the curving front of the defenders from Teruel eastward to the sea.

1938-09-13.text: LONDON, Sept. 15. UP— Events in Europe moved rapidly towards a climax tonight which seemed to threaten at any time the spark that might set off an explosion in Czechoslovakia. The British government, stunned by the import of the ultimatum, held an urgent meeting at No. 10 Downing Street— a war preparedness meeting not excelled since 1914.

Nurnberg, Sept. 13—(AP)—German Nazis looked beyond Adolf Hitler's Nurnberg address today and saw only one, inevitable end: the German absorption of 3,500,000 Sudeten Germans of Czechoslovakia. The chancellor, as Nazis summarized his speech, stood firm against British and French pressure with a promise of aid when needed by the Sudeten Germans; he left the way open for peaceful settlement by admonishing the Prague government to negotiate an understanding with the Sudetens. He did not in specific words say that armed force would be used to assure the right of “self-determination” to the Sudetens; but he announced the building of great new fortifications on the French frontier. Hitler Enunciates Policy The chancellor enunciated his policy, without narrating specific details of future action, in four portions of his 78-minute address closing the tenth annual Nazi party rally yesterday. Nurnberg, Germany, Sept. 12 (7%) ~Reichsfuehrer Hitler in one of the greatest oratorical efforts of his life threw down the gauntlet to England and France tonight, asserting that come what may Germany is determined to liberate the Sudeten Germans, ~ Hitler’s promise of aid to the 3,500,000 Sudetens in Czechoslovakia was unconditional. WILL “HELP” SUDETENS, “I assure the democracies that the fate of the Sudetens is not a matter of indifference to us,” he said challengingly. ‘If these harassed people feel they are without rights and aid they will get both from us.” “The Almighty did not create 3,500,000 Sudeten Germans to deliver them over to a hated foreign regime,” Hitler shouted at the closing of the tenth annual Nazi party rally in a speech which the world had awaited, “The Almighty has not created 7,000,000 Czechs to act as the guardians of these Germans.” LEAVES COURSE IN DARK. LONDON, Sept. 12.—Competent British observers said tonight Chancellor Adolf Hitler in his Nurnberg speech had virtually demanded that the Sudeten German minority of Czechoslovakia be allowed to set up their own state within a state. According to this interpretation, Chancellor Hitler gave Britain a choice of forcing Czechoslovakia to permit such a move, or of standing firm with France in a war-fraught challenge to Germany. This was the way observers read the German Fuehrer's demand that the Sudeten Germans be given their "rights." Official reaction was lacking as Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s three key ministerial advisers surrounded him in No. 10 Downing Street tonight to weigh the implications of the speech. These ministers were Viscount Halifax, foreign secretary; Sir John Simon, chancellor of the exchequer, and Sir Samuel Hoare, home secretary. But it was clear to informed per

PARIS, Sept. 12—The French government viewed Chancellor Adolf Hitler’s Nurnberg speech tonight as a virtual threat to resort to armed forces unless France and Great Britain compel Czechoslovakia to turn over her Sudeten German regions to Nazi Germany. Declaring the Reichsfuehrer’s speech increased tension in Europe and promises many weeks of armed alertness, a Foreign Office official asserted the only relief to be drawn from Chancellor Hitler’s words was that “war is postponed for the moment.” It was announced even while the Fuehrer’s speech was pouring into Paris that tomorrow's cabinet meeting with President Albert Lebrun would consider further reinforcement of the nation's defenses and measures to protect the civil population.

LONDON, Sept. 13—The board of Lloyd's, the underwriters, was summoned today to meet Thursday to discuss a proposal to cease quoting war risks altogether. Already such insurance is limited largely to the marine field.

New York, N. Y., Sept. 13—CP—Rep. Robert Low Bacon, 54, a republican congressman since 1922 and member of a family socially and politically prominent in New England for generations, died of a heart attack last night. The congressman, representing the first district, second largest in the United States, had been unopposed for renomination in the republican primary Sept. 20. His widow and two daughters survive. He will be buried Thursday in Arlington cemetery, Washington, D.C.

GENEVA, Sept. 13 (4).—The League of Nations’ round table was cleared as a sounding board today for Great Britain and France after Adolf Hitler's attack on Czechoslovakia. A Russian spokesman called the Nazi tactics “a bluff to carry the crisis along until Germany is ready for action,” and urged Geneva as a logical place for a “reply to Nuremberg” when Chancellor Hitler spoke yesterday.

1938-04-24.text: LONDON, April 23 (—Treasury experts ended their search today for more revenue to meet heavily increased rearmament and other costs in the fiscal year which began April 1. The public will not know from whose pocket the cash will come until Tuesday, when Sir John Simon, chancellor of the exchequer, presents the 1934-89 budget to the House of Commons. Britain faces the necessity of raising millions of pounds sterling additional for rearmament under the handicaps of slowly declining business and a tax rate already the highest in her history. The cabinet will be given the budget. See BRITISH, Page & Col 6

VIENNA, April 23 (P.--Jews in Vienna were forced today to picket their own stores. Jewish shopkeepers were made to hold upwards at arm’s length signs reading “Don't Buy From Jews.” Draped about the necks of persons found in Jewish establishments were placards proclaiming: “This stupid, common person still purchases at Jewish stores.” Hundreds of SA ‘brownshirt’ Hitler youth directed the mass anti-Jewish boycott while German officials began a purge of the famed Austrian National Library. The chief librarian was supplied with a list of proscribed “non-Aryan” works to be removed and burned from the 1,200,000 volumes in the magnificent collection. Destroyed or relegated to cellars were the works of Thomas Mann, Stefan Zweig, Jacob Wassermann. In the picketing of Jewish stores, Nazis put up signs, warning, “Aryans, do not buy from Jews.” Windows of a leading coffee shop were smeared with thre

SHANGHAI, April 24. (Sunday) (P)—A Japanese army spokesman said today the Rising Sun banner had been carried across the border into Kiangsu Province when the reorganized Japanese offensive drove a deep wedge into Chinese lines in Southern Shantung. The Japanese salient, he said, was a few miles east of Taierhchwang, where the invaders suffered a smashing defeat April 6 after they had occupied the city and crossed the border into Kiangsu for the first time from the north. Twenty thousand Chinese were reported retreating in the direction of Pihsien, about eight miles from the Lunghai railway, a vital east-west line, which the Japanese have been trying to reach for months. Japs Hard Hit The Chinese asserted the Japanese offensive suffered a serious setback in vicious fighting north of Taierhchwang, where 5,600 Japanese troops who escaped from besieged Yihsien attempted to join the main colu

' HENDAYE, France (At the Spanish Frontier), April 23 (0) Spanish insurgents announced tonight they had broken through government lines in three places in a new drive on the Teruel front. They reported capture of the highway city of Aliaga, in the San Just mountains 32 miles northeast of Teruel, on the front some 160 miles east of Madrid. (Government military dispatches from Bourg-Madame, on the French-Spanish border, said 2,000 insurgent troops had been trapped in a Pyrenees pass and wiped out by eighty government gunners operating from Maladetta mountain. The attack took place in a ravine below Viella. Other insurgents continued to hold the Aran valley, but the 43rd division, cut off from the main government army a few days ago, restored its communication lines and presented a sudden threat to the insurgent rear guard. (UP) —Nationalist forces widened the wedge between Barcelona and Madrid along the entire southern front today, capturing the city of Aliaga, 23 miles north of Teruel and driving down the coastal highway on Castellon de la Plana. Nationalist troops of Gen. Miguel Aranda smashed a formidable loyalist concentration on the coast highway and occupied Alcala de Chisbert after which they continued towards Castellon, halfway between Benicarlo and Valencia. Nationalist headquarters announced that Gen. Bautista Sanchez’s troops captured the city of Aliaga at 6 p. m. and continued to advance to the south, wiping out the long pocket which extended from the sea back to Teruel. BOMBAY, April 23 (AP)—Frail, despondent Mohandas K. Gandhi, who has led India’s millions along the troublesome road toward political autonomy, has predicted his own early death. “My days are numbered,” the 68-year-old Mahatma wrote in the newspaper Harijan. “I am not likely to live very long—perhaps a year or a little more,” he said Saturday.

NEW YORK, April 25—Roosevelt hospital officials disclosed today that Brig. Gen. Charles Gates Dawes, former vice president who was taken suddenly ill yesterday, had been operated on for “acute suppurative appendicitis.” Dawes, who will be 73 years old on Aug. 27, came to New York from Chicago to attend the wedding of Francis Warren Pershing, son of Gen. John J. Pershing, and Muriel Bache Richards.

W GRUNDY, Va., April 23—(AP)—Forty-five charred and broken bodies of miners were taken from the seared depths of the Keen Mountain mine of the Red Jacket Coal Company today, victims of the volcano-like explosions which greeted the night shift as it entered the mine yesterday. The United States Bureau of Mines officials said no further bodies were in the "drifts" which extend far under the mountain. Mine rescue squads worked in thirty-minute relays in the furnace-like atmosphere until they had explored every avenue of the big mine. Two members were overcome by bad air which had to be blown out before the final group of bodies could be removed. Work For Hours For many hours the crews worked grimly, without hope of finding life among the victims trapped by the blast, but unwilling to cease their efforts until every miner had been accounted for. Attorney Lamar Hardy, without explanation, brought the missing document into court. London, Oct. 27-(4)-Egal Stanhope, president of the board of education, was named first lord of the admiralty today to succeed Alfred Duff Cooper, who resigned Oct. 1 because of “distrust” of Prime Minister Chamberlain’s foreign policy. Tokyo, Oct. 27-(4)-The United States note demanding that “unwarranted interference” with American rights in China be stopped, will not be published in Japan. Although the note specifically requested a prompt reply, the Japanese foreign office said no definite date for answering it had been set. LONDON — Preliminary steps have been taken toward a new conference between Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and Fuehrer Adolf Hitler of Germany—this one on a sweeping program of European appeasement, it was said in a most reliable quarter today. Initiative is being taken by the British government, it was said, as the result of a report to the cabinet by Sir Neville Henderson, British ambassador to Germany, that there was a good outlook for a permanent British-German understanding on the basis of all-around European appeasement. Informants said the cabinet had given its full approval to a Chamberlain-Hitler meeting and that it was most likely that King George, in his speech from the throne at the opening of the new session of parliament Nov. 8 would hint at the probability of such a conference. Europe’s dictatorial powers received the President's attack on use of force and persecution of “helpless wanderers” with resentment. In Rome, Fascist circles criticized the speech for implying that the totalitarian states were entirely to blame for the rearmament race. Britain, France and Geneva received the speech enthusiastically but with only dim hope it might lead to an arms conference. He spoke of the crisis over Czechoslovakia and President Roosevelt's contribution in appeals for peace, a contribution which he said was as “valuable as it was welcome.” “Most deeply do we appreciate what the president and Cordell Hull, secretary of state, have done and will continue to do in the cause of peace,” he said. Speaking of the United States neutrality legislation he said ‘we do not question the motive, and ‘no one on this side expects you to do anything which we have the sense to know to be impossible. Haifa, Palestine. Oct. 26. (P)— Several thousands of Britain's best troops today began the biggest military operation in Palestine since the arrival of reinforcements with an intensive drive against Arab rebels in the districts of Acre and Galilee. Preceded by land “minesweepers,” armored cars, and wireless wagons, detachments of troops with light mountain artillery, machine-guns, rifles and bombs moved into the area of 300 square miles under the command of Brigadier General John Francis Evetts, new military governor of the Galilee district. By courtesy of the British high command, along with a group of other newspaper correspondents, I joined the advancing column as it moved through this worst of rebel-infested sections with its rolling hills, broad valleys and sprawling stone villages. I saw British forces proceed to blow up with dynamite about a dozen houses in an Arab village from wh

LONDON (UP)—Lloyd’s shipping agency correspondent at Kobe, Japan, reported today that the American Dollar Liner President Coolidge was slightly damaged there today when it struck a wharf. The liner was detained by Japanese authorities at Shanghai, on its way to Japan and the United States, until $4,500,000 worth of Chinese silver, consigned to the Chase National Bank, at New York, was removed. By GRATIAN McGROARTY (United Press Staff Correspondent) WASHINGTON— The United States has informed the Japanese government that she finds it increasingly difficult to ‘reconcile’ herself to the trade situation which Japan has created in China, the State Department announced today. A governmental note charged that Japan had been responsible for ‘arbitrary and illegal’ acts to the detriment of United States nationals and United States trade. It contrasted Japanese promises with Japanese performances

London, Oct. 26.——The British cabinet has taken a further step toward European appeasement, it was reported tonight to have agreed to put into operation soon the long-dormant Anglo-Italian pact arranged last Easter. The cabinet was reported to have made this decision despite a warning by wartime Prime Minister David Lloyd George, who said that Britain, as a result of the Munich pact, was heading for “a war without friends.” Reliable sources said they understood the cabinet had decided the agreement sealing Prime Minister Chamberlain's friendship with Premier Mussolini would come into force between Nov. 13 and Nov. 30 after the new session of parliament, convening Nov. 1, has had time to debate it. The cabinet took its stand in a wide review of the empire's problems, from Germany's sweeping colonial claims to English trade, at the very moment Lloyd George was flaying Britain's treatment o

1938-04-08.text: LONDON, April 6, Britain has informed Mexico she considers expropriation of foreign oil companies “inherently unjustified” and has requested restoration of the holdings of the British-owned Aguila Company. (Aguila, owned by Royal Dutch Shell, was the largest of the 17 American, British, and Dutch companies in the $400,000,000 industry taken over by President Lazaro Cardenas on March 18.) Informed persons said Britain had under consideration possible steps to enforce its stand, but declined further comment. They said it was “presumed” Mexico now would do something about the situation.

Great Britain began maneuvers to stabilize European peace today in front of a French cabinet crisis and steady gains by insurgent armies in Spain's civil war. While the cabinet of French Premier Leon Blum was crumbling, British "personalities" were reported to have opened negotiations with Edouard Daladier, expected to be the new government leader, for extension of immediate credit. Whether such negotiations would succeed was highly doubtful. In return for the credit it was said that Daladier would ask to form a strong cabinet, avoiding any communist participation, collaborating with Britain in keeping hands off Spain, and permitting the French-Russian alliance to lapse. At Paris, Premier Blum’s leftist government resigned, balked by the Senate in its demand for extraordinary powers to bring about financial recovery. Meanwhile the Spanish nationalist armies were forced to call up reinfor

LONDON, April 7.--(AP)--Three Royal Air Force fliers were killed today when their reconnaissance plane exploded and fell into the North Sea. The Air Ministry officially identified the plane which had been the object of a widespread search near Dudgeon Light, off the Humber estuary, where it was seen to burst into flame. Searchers found only oil patches and bits of wreckage. The crash was the 34th in the Royal Air Force since January 1, and raised its death toll to 58 since then. The plane had been on a night routine navigation flight and last had radioed all well.

The Associated Press Extensive damage to orchards and power networks was reported Thursday in the broad area swept by spring storms. Fresh snow plagued 12 states from Texas to New England as thousands of laborers struggled to clear highways buried under Wednesday's heavy fall. Storms In South For the second consecutive day, tornadoes dipped into the South. Ten people were killed at Aliceville, Ala. More than a score were treated in improvised hospitals. Several residents were reported missing. Five persons were injured when a twister destroyed their home near Philadelphia, Miss. Weather bureau officials at Washington said the abrupt return of winter weather would cause considerable damage to fruit, garden and other early crops in the eastern and central sections although it should benefit wheat. Sleet, rain and snow wrought new havoc in Ohio. Losses on fruit farms and along utility lines

Kobe, Japan, April 8. Admirai Yonai, minister of the navy, declared today that the announced decision of the United States and Britain to abandon the 35,000-ton battleship limits of the 1936 London treaty must “be interpreted as evidence of their intention to oppose Japan.” He declared Japan was not building “bigger ships at present,” but said the American and British programs might compel her to revamp her naval program.

LONDON, April 8 —The government, protesting today against the expropriation of British oil wells in Mexico, told the Mexican government that it “must formally request the restoration of properties belonging to the Mexican Eagle Company.” The protest described the expropriation as “inherently unjustified.”

(Associated Press Affairs Editor) NEW YORK, April 8 ()—British Labor has administered a face-reddening rebuke to Premier Chamberlain and his dominant conservative party by electing a member to parliament on a platform of condemnation for the government’s policy towards the dictators. The laborites won under an anti-cabinet slogan of “Back to the League of Nations, or get out.” They claim the harassed Chamberlain is inviting war by dicker- ing with the dictators instead of “giving them the works” through a resuscitated league. Naturally British labor doesn’t want war, but labor holds no copyright on a desire for peace. The conservatives hate war too. Both of them have good reason to know its horror, for it was burned into the memories of many of them on the battlefield.

CHICAGO, April 8. (4)—European nations led by Great Britain made their heaviest single day's buying of wheat in months today and as a result world prices soared 3 to 4 cents a bushel. Total purchases in the international market including the United States, Canada, Australia and Argentina were estimated by traders as high as 10,000,000 bushels, a sharp contrast to recent hand-to-mouth takings from abroad. Reports indicated the United Kingdom acquired 13 to 20 cargoes of Australian wheat, four cargoes of new Canadian grain for fall shipment, three cargoes from Argentina and seven to nine cargoes of United States hard winter grain. Continental nations were understood to have bought 800,000 bushels of hard winter. Greece also was reported in the market.

1938-04-06.text: LONDON, April 5 (UP)—Five men were killed today in a Royal Air Force bomber crash at Tibthorpe, Yorkshire. The bomber had been on a night flight. It was the thirty-second RAF crash since Jan. 1, with a total of 52 deaths. Intensive training under the rearmament spec. up was generally ascribed as the reason for the large number of accidents.

COLUMBUS— (UP)— Frank L. Brothers, age 50, once head of the conservation division accounting section, died today from a lung ailment which in January brought him a parole from the London Prison Farm where he was sent in June, 1936, for embezzlement of $13,000 in state funds.

MEXICO CITY, BpreewwyT Archbishop Garibi y Rivera, of Guadalajara, yesterday called upon Mexican Catholics to raise a fund to help pay 17 American and British oil companies for their $400,000,000 holdings expropriated by the government March 18. This move, approved by Archbishop Luis Martinez, of Mexico City, came as oil companies asked in district court for an injunction against enforcement of a federal labor board terminating their labor contracts with their 18,000 former employees. Archbishop Martinez promised a pastoral letter on the oil controversy during holy week. The oil workers’ union said yesterday its members were prepared to contribute a day's pay each month “as long as needed” to help pay for the expropriated property.

NEW YORK, April 5 (P)—A group of German and Austrian refugees arrived Tuesday on the British liner Antonia to accept this country's historic and recently renewed offer of political asylum. They came as millions who now are Americans had come in years past—through the narrows and on up the shining bay past the Statue of Liberty, gleaming in the April sun. As the coast guard cutter Calumet pulled alongside the Antonia and the ladder was put for the officers to clamber aboard for the customary inspections, some of the silent few who lined the Antonia's upper deck smiled and held up their hands in tentative greeting. But for the most part the arrivals were a stolidly quiet and bewildered lot. Most, of course, could speak no English and the exact number who could be classified as actual fugitives from their homelands was impossible of determination. BARACOA, Cuba —(P)— The captain and five members of the crew of the British schooner Jominx reached this port today in a lifeboat after their ship struck drifting wreckage and sank 20 miles off Maisi Lighthouse. The schooner was bound for Nassau with a cargo of salt.

Rome. April Ant lohe proposed Walian-English friendship treaty will bind Italy to withdraw troops from Spain after—but not before—the civil war is over, informed quarters said tonight. Italy has agreed to retire troops also from the strategically important islands in the Mediterranean at the same time, these sources said, after another meeting between the negotiators, the British ambassador and the Italian foreign minister.

London, Apr. 5 (#)—The Spanish government protested to France and Great Britain tonight against continuation of their non-intervention policy with its “appalling and dangerous injustice.” The government note recalled Spain’s messages of March 22 charging a renewal of German and Italian aid to Spanish insurgent armies which now have split Catalonia from the rest of government Spain. Agitation grew in Wales for a national coal strike to demand that the government drop its “hands off Spain” policy and allow the Spanish government to buy British munitions.

LONDON, April 5,~- (i — The house of commons tonight approved and sent to the house of lords a bill calling for public control of Great Britain's coal industry. The measure provides that eventually the government would assume ownership of all coal resources in Great Britain through purchase of privately owned coal royalties and voluntary and compulsory amalgamation of collieries. There are between 4,000 and 5,000 owners of coal royalty rights, collecting a fee on each ton of coal produced. Under the bill, the government would pay royalty owners about $22,350,000 a year for 15 years, a total of $332,250,000. Payments to individual royalty owners would be made on the basis of valuation as of Jan. 1, 1939, and the government would assume coal ownership July 1, 1942. 1938-10-04.text: London, Oct. 4 (AP).—Earl Baldwin, Neville Chamberlain's predecessor as Prime Minister, today endorsed Chamberlain's Munich accord while the angry opposition renewed its assault on that pact for the dismemberment of Czechoslovakia. Baldwin, in his maiden speech in the House of Lords, declared that “when the Prime Minister took that decision to go to Berchtesgaden, there was nothing else on earth he could have done, and I thank God that he was able to do it.” While Baldwin spoke the Labor opposition in the House of Commons bitterly assailed Chamberlain for the four-power Munich agreement. It was the second day of debate on the Prime Minister's policies. The debate is expected to continue through tomorrow when the government will present a motion approving the Prime Minister's actions in Europe's recent war scare. Daughters of the American Revolution from various sections of the State asse

MADRID, Oct. 4 — Three British ships were struck by bombs today and two of them set afire in a renewal of Spanish insurgent air raids along the Mediterranean coast of government Spain. Fourteen Savoia (Italian) type planes in a raid on the Barcelona waterfront bombed and set on fire the Theorpebay, 2,182 tons, and the Gothic, 2,146 tons. No casualties were reported. In Valencia harbor, a lone seaplane dropped 12 bombs, one of which struck the 1,074-ton British vessel Luimneach. The ship’s cook, said to be British, was injured. In another seaplane raid, several buildings were destroyed at the port of Denia.

London.- Wind reaching 93 miles an hour in some sections lashed the British Isles and caused eight deaths during the night. A large tree crushed a South London double-decker bus and killed three. The other deaths were in rural accidents. The wind snapped telephone and telegraph wires, wrecked small houses and drove ashore many light craft.

London, Oct. 4—(CUP)—A Reuters, British news agency dispatch from Prague tonight reported that the Czechoslovak government under General Jan Syrovy had resigned. The government will be reconstituted with Syrovy continuing as premier, the dispatch said. The resigning government was informed by Syrovy, inspector general of the Czechoslovak army, when former Premier Milan Hodza resigned September 22 during the Sudeten crisis.

By The Associated Press London, Oct. 3.—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain drove home to his sombre House of Commons today his blunt belief that four men at Munich—Hitler, Mussolini, Daladier and himself—saved civilization “as we have known it.” He steadfastly backed all he had done. Voices of dismay, humiliation and rage preceded and followed his 55-minute address, explaining and justifying the accord at Munich, which dismembered Czechoslovakia. Alfred Duff Cooper, the man who until Saturday was Chamberlain's First Lord of the Admiralty, sobbed as he cried out that the price of peace at Munich “stuck in my throat.” Proud Of Feat But Chamberlain replied: “I have nothing to be ashamed of. Those who have may hang their heads.” He praised President Roosevelt and the contributions of Daladier, Mussolini and Hitler. Chamberlain announced the quick $50,000,000 loan for Czechoslovakia. London — U.P. — The labor party told Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain in the House of Commons today that Great Britain’s position was “more dangerous” than ever as a result of the Munich peace agreement, on which the government demanded a vote of confidence. Herbert Morrison, laborite, said that Britain was likely in the future to face either submission to Adolf Hitler or a “straight fight” in which Britain and France — without allies — would oppose Germany and Italy. The parliamentary labor party earlier had decided to introduce an amendment to the government motion for a vote of confidence, asserting its relief that war had been averted “for the time being” but opposing approval of a policy that led to the “sacrifice of Czechoslovakia under the threat of armed force and to the humiliation of our country and its exposure to grave danger.” Political observers did not regard the labor a

LONDON, Oct. 4—(UP)—Gales reaching 76 miles an hour lashed the coast during the night and this morning, disrupting shipping and causing several casualties. Three omnibus passengers were killed and eight hurt in upper Norwood when a huge elm tree crashed onto the top deck. Air service between London and Paris was halted this morning.

By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS Adolf Hitler went ahead today with his triumphal tour of Sudetenland, while the British and French governments defended the roles they played in giving him his bloodless victory. Britain’s prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, faced an angry opposition for the second successive day and heard his “peace with honor” Munich accord bitterly assailed by Major Clement R.K. Attlee, Herbert Morrison and other Labor leaders. The government expected to end the debate tomorrow, when it will present a motion approving Chamberlain’s actions. Premier Edouard Daladier, addressing a special session of the French parliament, announced a new era of friendly relations with Germany and Italy. Hitler, speaking in the world-famed spa, Karlsbad (Karlovy Vary), told a Sudeten German audience, “I didn’t know how I would sometime get here, but I did know that I would come.” He told the crow

PARIS—French cabinet ready if war comes; may move capital to interior if Paris is threatened, and evacuate civilians; more troops moved to frontier; many residents evacuate families from border regions and withdraw funds from banks. Copyright 1938 by United Press LONDON, Sept. 12 (WP)— The United States cruiser Nashville steamed into Portland harbor today as Europe faced a climactic day in the Czechoslovak problem. The Nashville fired a 21-gun salute and the British battleship Royal Oak responded. It was a scheduled arrival for the Nashville, and the cruiser Honolulu is due at Grovesend, down the Thames from London, Sept. 22, also on a scheduled visit. But the movements of the crack American cruisers at this time lent emphasis to the persistent belief, despite deprecatory statements in the United States, that America is taking a strong and friendly role in support of Great Britain and France in their efforts to save Europe from war. LONDON, Sept. 12.—The Duke of Windsor may return from exile to attend the funeral of his cousin, and favorite relative, Prince Arthur of Connaught, sources close to Buckingham Palace told the United Press today. The prince died in his sleep of a gastric ailment. He was one of the least known members of the royal family, but was an intimate friend of the former king. They were brother Masons. Palace sources said the duke undoubtedly would desire to return for the funeral. The royal family would wish it or at least would put no obstacles in the way, it was said. No mention was made of whether his duchess, the former Wallace Warfield, could return with him without objection. The prince was the only son of the Duke and Duchess of Connaught. The Duke of Connaught is a son of Queen Victoria. In 1913 Prince Arthur married his cousin, Princess Alexandra, Duchess of Fife in her own right and co-h

London, Sept. 11.--(#)--The British government, recognizing the imminent danger of war, was said reliably today to have stressed to Germany the futility of expecting Britain to stay out of any conflict in which French integrity was involved. A definite commitment to aid Czechoslovakia in the event that country were invaded was withheld, responsible British quarters said Sir Nevile Henderson, British ambassador to Berlin, had told German leaders emphatically that they could not count on a brief campaign with Britain and France not involved. The British dominions and the United States kept fully informed of developments. United States Ambassador Joseph P. Kennedy saw Viscount Halifax, British foreign secretary, during the afternoon and called on Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain tonight. (By United Press.) Europe, armed for war, waited today for a fateful word from Adolf Hitler. Britain and France, like Germany, were enmeshed in a dispute which has grown like a rolling snowball, and peace or war hung on whether either side could afford to draw back, having gone so far. War was in the air. Millions talked of nothing else. Every country worked feverishly to protect itself if war comes. The British cabinet, having told Hitler that if he invades Czechoslovakia, Britain will fight with France, discussed final arrangements for naval, military, and aerial warfare. Czechoslovakia, determined to fight rather than submit to German encroachment, informed Britain in decisive terms that she will not stand for a plebiscite. France made every last-minute preparation for possible war. More troops poured back of the Maginot line facing Germany. Citizens sent their families to the interio

Nurnberg—Adolf Hitler hints strongly that German absorption of Czechoslovakia’s Sudeten region alone can satisfy Nazi demands in an address to 110,000 uniformed Nazis, London—Britain emphatically warns Germany not to count her out of any conflict involving France, reliable quarters report; cabinet to weigh situation Monday. Prague—Czechoslovaks await anxiously Hitler's Nurnberg speech Monday, next anticipated critical turn in minorities dispute; resentment flares over Field Marshal Goering’s reference to republic as “midget people without culture” who oppress and molest Sudeten Germans. Paris—France strengthens virtual war-time status; defenses buttressed on German frontier; railroad workers in eastern France get gas masks along with instructions to be alert for wartime duties.

NUREMBERG, Germany, Sept. 12. (UP)—Adolf Hitler defied Great Britain and France tonight to prevent Germany from assuring self-determination for Sudeten Germans in Czechoslovakia. "If the Sudeten Germans cannot defend themselves they will receive help from us," he declared. Hitler made no threats in his speech, merely laying down the principle that Germany must defend the Sudetens. He did not indicate how Germany would proceed, but gave hints of possible insistence on a plebiscite by his declaration for self-determination. However, he also pointedly called attention to Germany’s military strength. Hitler outlined at length the strength of German fortifications, linking it with his forthright declaration that oppression of the Sudetens "must end."
