ROME, Oct. . $< BP)—A British-Italian agreement to liquidate outstanding disagreements is imminent, it was reported today in most reliable quarters. It was even predicted that agreement might be reached by tomorrow night. The Earl of Perth, British ambassador, and Count Galeazzo Ciano, foreign minister, had their third talk within three days this morning. Make Progress It was understood that they made further progress toward an agreement which would: 1.—Bring the withdrawal of Italian troops from Spain. 2.—Result in bringing into effect the British-Italian pact, concluded in April but hinged on the withdrawal of Italian troops from Spain. 3.—Result in British recognition of Italy’s conquest of Ethiopia, which also was part of the friendship treaty.

Washington, Oct. 4.—(AP)—Senator King (D., Utah) said today last week's developments in Europe might make it necessary for the United States to ‘spend hundreds of millions of dollars more for military purposes.’ He said Great Britain and France, by ‘a spineless attitude’ toward Adolf Hitler, had “strengthened the forces which make for war and the domination of peoples and nations.” For that reason, he was of the opinion America must take every defensive precaution. More Hopeful With this view, however, Senator Bulkley (D., Ohio) partially disagreed. It is too early to determine the consequences of the Munich settlement of the Czech-German territorial dispute, he said, but at least the prospects for disarmament seem “more hopeful.” Senator Logan (D., Ky.) sided with King, asserting the outcome of the European crisis had made it essential that “our national defense program be carried out w

LONDON —UP— Seventeen persons were killed and many injured in a gale which swept Great Britain Monday night and throughout yesterday, it was determined today. Many ships were washed ashore. Numerous houses were damaged. Thousands of telephone lines were disrupted. Rivers overflowed in some areas flooding roads and marooning automobiles.

London, Oct. 4. (4) — Sir Thomas Inskip, defense coordinating minister, told the House of Commons tonight Britain would feel morally bound to aid Czechoslovakia in event of unprovoked aggression although technically Britain’s guarantee of her in the Munich accord in which Britain and France guaranteed Czechoslovakia’s short frontiers, Sir Thomas said if the Czechs were attacked “his majesty’s government would feel it necessary to take steps to see that the integrity of Czechoslovakia is preserved.

Oball VORrrespunawner London, Oct. 5—Premier Mus- solini, pressing swiftly toward re- construction of Europe’s political scene, today demanded immediate application of the Anglo-Italian agreement, including recognition of his conquest of Ethiopia. This was revealed as the British government prepared to plunge into still another session of the heated House of Commons debate on European affairs and the Munich agreement for dismemberment of Czechoslovakia. Il Duce forged his demand with the British government, it was learned, under the implied threat that otherwise he will resort to large-scale intervention in the Spanish civil war, thus tipping the balance heavily in favor of the insurgents. 1938-05-01.text: LONDON, April 26 (AP)—It is Adolf Hitler’s move in the European game which may involve war or another change in the map. Little Czechoslovakia, the republic born in the World War, is the danger spot. There, with May Day to be celebrated Sunday, the government banned political demonstrations in an effort to prevent possible racial and party clashes at a time when Konrad Henlein, leader of the country's minority of 3,500,000 Germans, is demanding a change in the nation’s foreign policy and autonomy for his followers. DUCE HOLDS BALANCE But the prime action this week is focused not in Praha but in Rome. Brisk Benito Mussolini there holds the balance of power, with one hand clasping Hitler’s in (Continued on Page 2, Col. 2)

LONDON, April 30. — Great Britain, firmly united with France in a new “London-Paris axis,” inaugurated a gigantic air force expansion program today and prepared for diplomatic and economic action in central Europe to back up the strongest defensive alliance since the World War. It was understood that the government aimed at a first line strength of about 3,000 fighting planes for the home defense forces alone, in addition to the planes of overseas units and the navy. What this means is plain when it is realized that every first line plane is backed by perhaps five reserve planes, so that a total home defense force — home defense includes defending Britain by attacking an enemy from the air — 18,000 planes is indicated. Until today, Britain had been aiming at a first line strength of 1,750 planes by March 1939. Aviation experts estimate that it will take Britain until 1940 to match German

WASHINGTON, (#)—Consultations between the United States and Britain to decide on the size of the new super-battleships each will build have reached a deadlock, officials said Saturday. Britain insists on a size limit of 42,000 tons. The United States insists that, in the present state of uncertainty as to the exact nature of Japan’s intentions, no limit at all could be set. The United States, as testified to before the Senate Naval Affairs Committee, wants battleships of 45,000 tons each—but she has not formally informed Britain of this fact. She has simply said no limit should be fixed. The United States’ consultants, Hershel V. Johnson, counselor of the London embassy, and Captain Russell Wilson, naval attache, met once with the British following formal announcement by both countries, dated March 31, of their intention to invoke the “escalator” clause in the London naval treaty of 1936

LONDON, April 30.—(#)—Britain’s average “Charley Citizen” with a $2,500 a year job in a city office, a wife, two children and a $4,000 suburban home works two months each year for the government. Professional calculators estimate that he pays one-sixth of his income in taxes, figuring in For a start the government takes $50 annual income tax. Another $60 based on the “rated” value of his home is assessed. Local government authorities take about $125 in “rates”—local taxes to maintain police, streets, poorhouses.

LONDON, April 30—(UP)— The Exchange Telegraph reported from Moscow today that three Russian Arctic airplanes had rescued 154 persons from three ice breakers which had been fast in the ice fields 500 miles from the Siberian coast since October. The rescued persons were flown in groups to the mainland. Thirty-three members of the ice breakers’ crews remained to man them until rescue ships could free them from the ice late this summer.

BERLIN, April 30.—(U.P)— Fuehrer Adolf Hitler may tell the world tomorrow what he thinks of the new “London-Paris axis,” it was indicated today. Hitler is to make two speeches on the occasion of the Nazi national labor holiday, which replaces the old left wing May Day. Germans and foreign diplomats awaited the speeches eagerly in the belief that they would indicate, if they did not show openly, what Hitler’s reaction has been to the unwritten military alliance between Germany’s two chief World War enemies.

-BOSTON, April 30.—(AP)—A last-minute ‘yes’ sped a New England maiden and her eager swain to the altar Saturday night for a marriage that promised to rival the fame of John Alden’s match with Priscilla. She made up her mind within a few hours of the midnight deadline set by her employer, a Boston utility, in a rule which said ‘Girls who marry on or after May 1 must quit their jobs.’ Her name was Miss Florence Rudolph, and the man she accepted was Harry C. McKenny. The best wishes of thousands of American women were with her, for unknowingly, she had become the symbol of the cause of the working girl. She was the fourth Boston maiden in a week to resort to a hasty wedding to escape loss of employment, and her job-holding sisters across the land were shouting: “It isn’t fair.” To this angry chorus, the new bride represented the goal of countless other girl employees who saw their chances o

Los Angeles, April 30 — A temporary restraining order was on file in superior court today against Lou Brice, brother of comedienne Fanny Brice, preventing him from collecting $130,000 which records showed he won from Harry T. Clifton of England in a single hand of stud poker. The order, issued by Superior Judge Emmet H. Wilson, held up paying of checks of $50,000 on a New York bank and $100,000 drawn on a London bank. Judge Wilson ordered a hearing next week. Named with Brice were three John Does, who sat in the game in a Long Beach hotel some time ago. Clifton, a frequent visitor in Southern California, later called in Attorneys Jerry Glesler and Paul Schreibman. The action complained the money was won by “trick and device” and that Brice did not have sufficient funds to cover the amount, had he lost. Attorney Glesler said Clifton staked the fortune on two pair. He explained he was only

1938-08-14.text: LONDON, Aug. 13. (2) — While alarms stalked through Europe today the British war office warned all Britons holding military rank that they must get special certificates in order to avoid “trouble” if and when they travel in Germany. France clamped down regulations virtually forbidding French citizens to go to Italy, whose relations with France have grown colder since Hitler’s Italian visit last May. Preparations Rushed. Germany hastened preparations for giant maneuvers next month of the regular army, already capable of overnight action. Residents on both sides of the German-Czechoslovak frontier were worried over German preparations for the giant maneuvers. Some said 1,000,000 men would participate in them. In London the continuing demand for gold mirrored European tension as buyers tried to get greater measures of security for their property. The gold price soared. Fortifications Rushed

Shanghai—Three Japanese soldiers were seized by United States marines today after a clash in the American defense sector of the international settlement. The encounter occurred during widespread disorders that swept Shanghai and involved both British and American sentries in incidents on patrol duty in the international settlement. The disorders marked the first anniversary of the outbreak of hostilities with Japan in the central China area. Two of the Japanese who defied the United States patrol were turned over to a representative of the Japanese army. The third, struck over the head when he resisted, was taken to a hospital. The men denied they were connected in any way with Japan's military forces but Japanese authorities acknowledged they were attached to the special service section of the Japanese army. Moreover, Germany, in a Berlin press release Saturday, sought to allay suspicion over the military exercises which are expected to reach their peak between September 9 and 14. | The press release, made available to all German newspapers by DNB, German official news agency, accused “interested foreign circles” of attempting “to stir up uneasiness in the European general public.” Nevertheless, the high government and military officials of other nations kept their staffs in a state of preparedness. LONDON. Aug. 13 (4%-~Overcoated children threw snowballs in Yorkshire today. In Norfolk the snow was two feet deep, the result of two days of freak storms that cut a crazy path across England and resulted in three deaths and property damage estimated at $7,500,000. At Wold Newton a number of women were hysterical because of the fury of lightning and thunder. Children fled screaming from an evangelist's tent when lightning struck the main pole and severely burned the preacher. Thousands of telephone lines were out of commission and hundreds of houses were struck by lightning. Laborers worked all night to remove tons of debris from railroad tracks. Many villages were flooded in northwest London; hailstones covered the ground to the depth of one inch.

LONDON, Aug. 13 (P)—Europe’s nerves were taut tonight with its worst attack of “war scare jitters” since armies faced each other across the German-Czech frontier three months ago, but governments of the big powers assured their people that “the next great war” still is distant. LONDON, Aug. 13.—U.P)—This was the day that European gossip had assigned for the beginning of the “next war.” It passed without a single explosive incident, although a series of foreboding developments kept nerves taut. European chancellories, although insisting that there was no cause for immediate alarm, remained alert in the knowledge that “anything can happen” during the next six or eight weeks. Developments included: Germany — Began mustering 1,000,000 or more men in arms for the biggest army maneuvers seen in Europe since the World War, but denied the move had any connection with German ambitions in Czechoslovakia. A survey of the situation in Germany indicated that Hitler, if he does spring a “surprise,” will probably delay it until late September or October. France—Restricted tourist travel to Italy in reprisal for a similar move by the Italian government. France said she saw no

LONDON, Aug. 13.—(7)—The little village of Wold Newton counted up a small fortune brought by a two-foot snowfall today while the rest of Britain surveyed its losses from two days of freak storms. Visitors flocked to the hamlet, near Bridlington in Yorkshire, in buses which solicited business with such provocative signs as: “Your chance to say you've seen snow in August.” Wold Newton urchins did a land-office business selling snow in old jam jars to the gullible. The price was two cents a jar.

LONDON, Aug. 18—(INS)—Persistent reports of mysterious moves of a military nature in Western, Southern and Southeastern Germany have caused Britain and France to agree upon a virtual joint plan of preparedness for any eventuality, International News Service learned today. Main feature of the new Anglo-French scheme is a close, joint diplomatic and consular watch within Germany during the next few weeks. Paris and London also will exchange information regarding anything they learn regarding Reich military maneuvers. Second, both the British and French general staffs will remain “in a state of special alertness” until the two governments are satisfied regarding Germany’s intentions. Third, both London and Paris will bring immediate diplomatic pressure upon Berlin at the first sign that Chancellor Hitler is preparing any sudden move in the direction of Czechoslovakia.

1938-11-13.text: LONDON, Nov. 12 (P)—Queen Mary listened with tears in her eyes tonight as she heard how her eldest son, David, the Duke of Windsor, pined to return to England with his American-born bride, the former Wallis Warfield Simpson. The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester, who visited the Windsors in Paris, reported to King George and later to the king’s mother on the prospects for a formal reconciliation of the former monarch and the royal family. The report was made coincident with disclosure that King George and Queen Elizabeth will leave for Canada on May 9 and will visit the United States the first week in June, probably from June 4 to 8. They will then return to Canada for a few days before going home. Details of their stay in the United States are not complete.

| LONDON, Nov. 12, U.P)—The “parallel” courses of the United States, Great Britain and France in international affairs appeared more distinct tonight as a result of developments in Germany, Chi- a and South America. Although it was emphasized in official sources that similar action is taken by the democracies only where similar interests happen to be involved, the darkening of prospects for international appease- ment as a result of the anti-Jewish action in Germany caused concern in liberal circles over Prime Min- ister Neville Chamberlain's pro- gram for dealing directly with the dictators and depending less on ties with democratic powers. PARIS, Nov. 12—(42—The Daladier government, backed by the demand of 7,000,000 World War veterans for a strong government, tonight issued 32 decree laws to rebuild France within her democratic framework. Premier Daladier declared they were the strongest measures that could be drawn without violating "traditional" principles of the French government. Some members of the Chamber of Deputies called them the last chance to avert collapse of the democracy. Among the laws decreed two days before expiration of semi-dictatorial decree powers granted by Parliament was a measure revaluing the gold reserve of the Bank of France at the rate of 170 francs to the pound sterling, or 37.69 to the dollar. The revaluation gave the government a paper profit of about 22,550,000,000 francs. Decrees drawn by the labor ministry did not officially change "the principle" of the 40-hour week, but said there would

BERLIN, Nov. 12—Nazi Germany today practically wiped out Jewish business, barred the nation’s 500,000 Jews from public entertainments and fined them $400,000,000 for the slaying of a German diplomat by a young Polish-German Jew in Paris. In addition, the government required that Jews whose 1,000 Berlin shops were wrecked or looted Thursday in mass demonstrations must pay for the damage themselves. Insurance claims by Jews for demolition of their properties must be paid to the state. Officials promised “further decisive measures” and Jews feared that the ghetto, unemployment or concentration camps were in store for them. Police made wholesale arrests among Jewish moneyed, educated and cultured classes, 1,600 being taken into custody in Berlin alone. In Vienna it was estimated that between 18,000 and 20,000 Jews had been arrested since Thursday. Many of them were released, but thousands st

The Nazi government on Saturday fined German Jews $400,600,000 and by a series of drastic decrees barred them from every gainful possession and occupation. The decrees and the mass fine designed to deprive 700,000 Jews of greater Germany of their economic and cultural rights were ordered by Fuehrer Adolf Hitler’s chief lieutenants to impose upon the entire community of German Jews as a whole a penalty for the base murder in Paris of Ernst von Rath, secretary of the German Embassy, by a Jewish youth. The decrees climaxed the destruction by organized Nazi bands of millions of dollars worth of Jewish property throughout the Reich. In addition to the huge fine, Jews by the decrees will be barred from retail and wholesale trade after January 1, they will not be permitted in theatres, at concerts, lectures, motion picture theaters, dance recitals and museums. Jews are forbidden to possess fire

BERLIN, Nov. 12.—(U.P)—Jews were practically eliminated from the economic and cultural life of Germany Saturday night by a series of Nazi measures which dealt them perhaps the severest blow since medieval times. The Nazi government, by a decree of Field Marshal Hermann Goering, imposed a collective fine of 1,000,000,000 marks ($400,600,000) on greater Germany’s 700,000 Jews in retaliation for the “cowardly murder” of a German diplomat by a Polish Jew in Paris. Methods of collecting the assessment were not revealed, but it was expected to wipe out a major part of Jewish financial interests in Germany. Another series of decrees barred Jews from every gainful profession and occupation. Immediate hunger was becoming acute in Austria. All Jewish stores were closed and ‘Aryan’ shopkeepers and restaurants were under orders not to sell food to Jews. The future was even more ominous. Saturday nig

NEW YORK, Nov. 12.—(#)—A drive for solidification of the nation’s progressive forces under President Roosevelt’s leadership was started today at the first of a series of conferences stemming directly from Tuesday's elections. Third term talk at the meeting of Mayor F. H. LaGuardia with two democrats, Governor Frank Murphy of Michigan and Senator Robert J. Bulkley of Ohio, both of whom failed of re-election, was denied. Murphy said afterward: “I think our minds should remain open on that entire question.” Bulkley said, however, he believed the people have a fixed opinion against a third term and “there is quite a sentiment against it.” Organization of a third party was frowned upon by Bulkley while Murphy emphasized a new policy would have to be formulated by leaders of the progressive movement and that it would have to center around President Roosevelt. NEW YORK, Nov. 12 (4)—The frail, wasted body of Mary Mallon, who in the hearty plumpness of her middle years became known as “Typhoid Mary,” innocent agent of death, was lowered into a grave in St. Raymond’s cemetery, the Bronx, today. The dubious fame of being known as the country’s oldest medical prisoner — officially isolated as typhoid carrier, No. 36 — had brought her bitterness and finally resignation. As the Rev. Vincent S. McCambley pronounced the last “requiem in peace,” there were only nine to whisper the response. For 31 years, since health officials, puzzled by recurring outbreaks of typhoid fever, discovered Mary was the source and plucked her from the living, she had remained in isolation, save for a brief period. 1938-02-04.text: Barcelona, Feb. 4. — () — The British freighter Alcira, trying to run the Spanish insurgent blockade, was bombed by two planes and sunk today 20 miles southeast of Barcelona. Her crew of 25 and an observer for the non-intervention control, all British, were rescued by a Spanish government sloop and fishing vessels and brought to Barcelona. A Barcelona communique said the planes came from the direction of Palma, Mallorca, insurgent naval and air base. Like the British freighter Kyndmion, sunk by an unidentified submarine off the Spanish east coast Monday, the Alcira was trying to carry a cargo of coal to a government port. The Alcira, 1,387 tons, left Gibraltar for Barcelona Jan. 31, under command of Captain M. McCracken of Glasgow. A trim figure in black, the woman counter-espionage agent who was identified only as "Miss X," unfolded her romantic story in court at a hearing for four men accused of copying plans smuggled out of the big Woolwich arsenal. Moscow Linked The defendants were remanded to Feb. 7 when “Miss X” corroborated the prosecution story of the alleged plot, which involved a mystery-shrouded couple named "Stevens" from Moscow. Glading, until 1928 an employee at the Woolwich arsenal; Albert Williams, former armament examiner at Woolwich; George Whomack, assistant foreman of the arsenal's gun section; and C. W. Ten persons were killed Monday when a torpedo sank the British freighter Endymion off Cartagena. It too, carried coal. In Tokyo, Foreign Minister Koki Hirota informed parliament that Japan had “warned other powers strictly to supervise shipments of arms and munitions to China.” He did not name the nations cautioned but said neither Italy nor Germany—allied with Japan against international communism—were materially aiding China. London, Feb 4—Causing Great Britain to consider plans for a naval blockade of Majorca, two Spanish insurgent planes bombed and sank the 1,387-ton British freighter Alcira off Barcelona today. The crew of 25 men and an officer appointed by the international non-intervention committee were saved by a Spanish fishing smack. The new outbreak of Mediterranean piracy occurred only a few days after the British freighter Endymion was torpedoed and sunk with a loss of eleven lives and served to increase British anger to the point of apoplexy. The Alcira flew the British flag and the neutral emblem of the non-intervention patrol. The new incident convinced British authorities that measures taken immediately after the Endymion sinking are insufficient to cope with piratical assaults in neutral shipping in the Mediterranean. 1938-01-05.text: SHANGHAI—A new and serious clash between Japanese and foreign interests was threatened today as Shanghai municipal authorities referred to the United States and British governments a Japanese demand for virtual control of the international settlement. Foreseeing a clash of interests, the Shanghai municipal government referred the Japanese demands to the United States and Great Britain through the American and British consulates general here. Settlement authorities planned to make no reply to the Japanese demands until they had received specific reaction from Washington and London. PAWTUCKET, R. I., Jan. 5 (® —Two hundred persons, mostly women, saved by spectacular rescue work, recovered today from the horror of a fire that trapped them during a beano party last night in the British-American hall. Thirty-seven, nine injured seriously, were treated for broken limbs, burns, bruises and gashes. Scores of others received first aid. The blaze—its origin still undetermined—broke out in the cellar and first floor of the hall, in the heart of the Pawtucket business district. Deputy Fire Chief William Connolly estimated damage at $25,000. Firemen carried about a hundred persons down ladders. Eight jumped from second story windows, fearful they would be pushed out. Others were tumbled down stairs by the rush for exits.

LONDON, Jan. 4—(UP)—Great Britain is preparing to send a delegation to the United States within two weeks to start negotiations for a trade pact between the two great democracies, it was reported today. Reports were that the board of trade, the treasury, the department of agriculture and probably the dominions office, as representing the dominions, would be included in the delegation along with foreign office experts. Conference Planned Belief was growing also that plans were being made for big scale international conferences, hinged on economic problems but designed actually to stop a drift toward war. Former Premier Paul Van Zeeland of Belgium, delegated by Britain and France to investigate the possibilities for an international economic conference, was reported to be ready to submit a report to the British government. PAWTUCKET, R. I. (AP). Turning American British hall into a roaring inferno, fire Tuesday night trapped approximately 200 persons attending a beano party and sent at least a score to two hospitals with serious burns, broken legs and arms. An hour later, after firemen brought the blaze under control, Pawtucket police expressed the belief that everyone had been removed from the building and that there had been no deaths. Running through flames into the smoke-filled building, firemen carried out scores of persons and brought at least 100 down ladders.

- PAWTUCKET, R. I., Jan. 4-- (AP) —Sweeping through big American British hall here, fire tonight trapped approximately 200 persons on the second floor. More than a score of persons went to two hospitals with injuries ranging from serious burns to broken limbs. Rushing to the blazing building with all available apparatus, firemen carried scores down ladders. The fire apparently started on the first floor and mushroomed rapidly upward. The hall, located in a two-story brick building in the business section, was the scene of a beano party. Approximately an hour after the fire started, firemen brought the blaze under control and police expressed belief everyone had been removed from the building. Shanghai, Jan. 5. (AP)—Chinese newspapers said today that 450 foreign volunteers were fighting with Chinese armies. They included 152 Americans, 124 French, 115 Russians and 55 British. It was assumed most of the Americans were aviators.

SHANGHAI, Jan. 5 (®)—Japanese authorities announced today they had taken over all Chinese government functions in the international city of Shanghai and other territory occupied by Japanese armies. A final step in Japan's drive for dominance was projected censorship of news dispatches. Japanese officials were said to have notified cable companies that Japanese censors were moving in to prevent leakage of military information to Chinese. For more than a month, dispatches have been free from interference. Chinese maintained some barriers until the fall of Shanghai. The disclosure that censorship would be imposed came shortly after Japanese officials raised what foreign authorities termed a “grave issue” by threatening action in the international settlement itself to halt “anti-Japanese outrages.” It coincided, also, with new advices by Japanese armies bent on consolidating control of five
Frankfort on the Main, Germany Jan. 4. (?)—Three passengers and three crew members, all Germans, were killed today when a Milan-on transport plane crashed on landing here.

1938-11-16.text: WASHINGTON, (AP). — State Department announced today the trade agreements with Great Britain and Canada would be signed at the White House tomorrow afternoon at 4 o'clock. Secretary of State Hull will sign for the United States. Canadian Prime Minister Mackenzie King will sign for Canada. The trade agreement with the United Kingdom was completed after six months of negotiation between a special delegation sent here by Great Britain and experts of the state and commerce departments. The British agreement brings the total number of trade agreements concluded to 19.

WASHINGTON. — British and American officials completed today the final details of the long-awaited Anglo-American trade treaty and the ceremony of signing it was expected to take place tomorrow. (At the same time, a new trade treaty between the United States and Canada will be signed. Both agreements have been negotiated simultaneously, a new Canadian treaty being necessary to eliminate conflicting trade commitments in empire agreements between Canada and Great Britain. The first American-Canadian treaty was signed in 1935 and has been operating successfully since. Drafts of the treaties—designed to increase trade and the economic and political ties of the largest groups of English speaking peoples of the world—were understood to be practically ready for official signatures. Rome, Nov. 16—(AP)—Italy emerged as the final victor today in the economic war England led against her during the Ethiopian campaign in 1935. By the two-nation peace understanding which became effective today, Britain formally recognizes the Ethiopian conquest and extends trade opportunities to the territory. By contrast, Britain with France sponsored the League of Nations fight which ended Oct. 22, 1935, when 52 league nations agreed to boycott Italian exports. The economic protest did not deter Italy from taking Ethiopia, but it did bring resentment against Britain, now ended by the British-Italian accord, and to a lesser degree against France. Soviet Russia and the United States are the only big powers who have not yet recognized the Ethiopian conquest. The United States did not participate in the economic boycott. Russia, as a Communist government, is not likely to give formal recogn

BERLIN, Nov. 16. — (U.P.) — The United States has made formal representations to the German government regarding damage done to American property during anti-Semitic riots. The representations, like those made by Great Britain, were in the form of a written note, in which the United States reserved all rights, including a demand for reparations. At least three claims have been made by American citizens. A fourth claim was understood to have been made from outside Berlin. Other countries have taken, or contemplate, similar action.

LONDON, Nov. 16 (UP) - A Five Power conference probably will be called to meet in London within a few days to discuss relief for Jews from Germany, it was indicated today. The nations involved would be the United States, Great Britain, France, the Netherlands and Brazil, composing the directorate of the Intergovernmental committee on refugees. The call for the meeting would be sent out by Lord Winterton, chairman of the committee, if the other four powers agree. In view of President Roosevelt's condemnation of the Nazi outbreak and the recent activity of Ambassador Joseph P. Kennedy on behalf of refugees, it was believed the United States would welcome the suggestion in the hope of helping Germany's 700,000 Jews.

PARIS, Nov. 16—The French and British governments, pushed to definite statements by rising parliamentary and public opinion, joined today in flat opposition to handing back colonies taken from Germany through the World War. The British attitude was bolstered by the statement of Gen. Jan Christiaan Smuts at Maritzburg, Natal, South Africa, that “we are going to defend South Africa and its vital interests, including Southwest Africa, to the uttermost.” Smuts was World War commander of the forces of the Union of South Africa. He termed the mandate over the 318,000 square miles of Southwest Africa, seized in 1915 from Germany and mandated by the League of Nations in 1920, a “sacred trust.” Smuts, former premier of the Union of South Africa, now is minister of justice of that British dominion. 1938-09-20.text: London, Sept. 19.—(4)—The governments of Britain and France today gave approval, apparently unanimous, to a tremendous international deal to satisfy Adolf Hitler and keep Europe’s great democracies out of war. With almost desperate finality the cabinets of London and Paris approved the decisions made by their premiers here yesterday, accepting Hitler’s demands on Czechoslovakia and proposing a system of guarantees which they hope will bring central European peace at the price of Czechoslovakia’s Sudetenland. The reply was delivered to the British and French governments through their legations here. As border hostilities spread, Great Britain was said to lack official information of the Czechoslovak government's stand on the joint British-French proposal to let Germany have the Sudeten areas. 1938-03-07.text: By The Associated Press LONDON—The admiralty dis- closed today that the British de- stroyers, Blanche and Brilliant, had been attacked—but not hit— by five unidentified bombing planes. The attack occurred yesterday off the Spanish coast in the same general area where the Spanish government fleet torpedoed and sank one of the insurgent prize cruisers. An admiralty official said he pre- sumed the attack on the British vessel was a result of the naval battle. He added, however, that it was obviously a case of mis- taken identity. The Blanche and the Brilliant were on Nyon patrol duty pro- tecting neutral shipping in the western Mediterranean against so- called “pirate” raids.

Madrid— (?) —Destruction of a crack 10,000-ton insurgent cruiser in a naval battle off Cartagena left a gaping hole today in the insurgent fleet blockade of Spanish government ports. (Reports to the London admiralty from the British destroyers Kempenfeld and Boreas said they rescued more than 400 men from the stricken ship before it sank in flames, ripped by a torpedo and pounded by aerial bombs. (These reports definitely identified the cruiser as the Baleares, whose normal complement was 765 men. The fate of others of the crew was not determined.) WHICH ONE UNKNOWN Spanish government authorities here had not determined whether it was the Baleares or her sistership, the Canarias, which was destroyed. Both were new—the Canarias was completed in 1935, the Baleares in 1937—and they were almost identical in appearance. Both participated in the battle yesterday. But regardless of which cruise

WASHINGTON, March 6. (14) -- President Roosevelt has challenged Great Britain's claim to two strategic islands in the Pacific by issuing an order placing them under the jurisdiction of this government's Interior department. His order directs the Interior department to take over, for administrative purposes, Canton and Enderbury islands in the Phoenix island group. They are within three degrees of the equator and are on the air route between the United States and Australia. Dispute over ownership of the two islands—and others in that general area—has existed for more than a century. Citizens of the United States, Great Britain and other countries have settled on islands in the Phoenix group since their discovery in the latter part of the 18th century. This government has let it be known it is prepared to begin discussions with Great Britain at any time looking toward settlement of the con

London, March 6 (#)—The immediate future of the British-engineered plan for a new Four-Power pact to secure European peace appears to depend on Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain's willingness to talk colonies with Germany's Foreign Minister, Joachim von Ribbentrop, this week. Observers attached more importance to the German’s visit than to the impending negotiations at Rome through Lord Perth, the British Ambassador. It was generally accepted that Von Ribbentrop, coming here Wednesday to take formal leave as German Ambassador, would say little more than hello and goodbye unless Chamberlain is ready to discuss reiterated German demands for colonies. But before Chamberlain could do this, it is generally believed, he would have to come to an agreement with France. Britain and France, close collaborators in foreign policy long before Chamberlain started his policy of dealing with dictators,

Moscow, March 7—(#)—Barbara Yakovleva, once a heroine of the Bolshevist revolution, came from prison today to testify against Nikolai Bucharin, like herself fallen from the highest ranks of Russia’s leadership. On the witness stand in Moscow’s greatest treason trial, Madame Yakovleva, a large, faded woman of 53, testified she heard in 1918 that Bucharin wanted Nikolai Lenin and Joseph Stalin assassinated if they insisted on peace with Germany. Madame Yakovleva, like Bucharin, was a close associate of Lenin in the early stages of the revolution. Once she was head of the dreaded Cheka, or secret police, and only last year she occupied for a time the post of commissar of finance, from which she went to prison. Her testimony, delivered nervously in a slow, weak, quavering monotone, was a high spot of the afternoon session of the trial of Bucharin and 20 others on charges of treason and murde

Shanghai, March 7—(4)—Japanese troops swept down the Shansi railway today to the extreme southwest corner of Shansi Province and, from six strategic “jumping off” points along the north bank of the Yellow River, struggled to cross into the heart of central China. The victorious drive southward through Shansi was climaxed by the capture of Chaotsun, railway terminus near the “Big Bend” of the Yellow River. Chaotsun is just across the mighty river from Tungkwan, on the important east-west Lunghai railway. Chinese forces defending the south bank of the river have resisted thus far, but military observers believe the Japanese are ready for a supreme effort. For days they have been “softening” Chinese resistance with incessant shell fire and airplane bombardment. These aviation and artillery attacks became more severe today, apparently to forestall any Chinese counter offensive and to clear t

BARCELONA, March 17.—Jubilant loyalist authorities planned a general naval offensive, it was reported today, as they celebrated their little fleet’s torpedoing of one of the two crack cruisers in the nationalist navy. Not only did they destroy the cruiser—either the Baleares or her sister ship Canarias, each of 10,000 tons—but their airplanes bombed other ships in the nationalist fleet. The cruiser, flames still smouldering in her blackened hull, was foundering off Cartagena while two British warships made for a nationalist port with approximately 400 survivors of an estimated crew of 765. The British warships braved a loyalist airplane attack on the nationalist fleet to rescue the survivors. The British ships were the flotilla leader Kempenfelt and the destroyer Boreas. Able Seaman George G. Long, of the Boreas, was fatally wounded by bomb fragments. Loyalist authorities were overjoyed

MADRID, March 6 (AP) - Spanish government warships torpedoed a 10,000-ton insurgent cruiser in a dramatic naval battle before dawn, leaving the shattered warship’s identity wrapped in flames Sunday off the Southeastern Coast of Spain. Government planes joined the sea engagement, 75 miles east of Cape Palos, in the Mediterranean, at daylight taking additional toll of the insurgent fleet. A government announcement identified the blazing warship as the insurgent Canarias, but the British admiralty, receiving reports from nearby British destroyers, said it was the Baleares, a cruiser of almost identical silhouette. Heavy Loss of Life Loss of life among the cruiser’s 765 crew was believed heavy although the British destroyers Kempenfelt and Boreas carried survivors from the cruiser to other insurgent war vessels. Both the Canarias and the Baleares, backbone of the insurgent fleet, carried com

1938-06-29.text: LONDON, June 29.—A double-barrelled inquiry involving questions of broad political significance threatened to weave new strands into the already tangled web of Britain’s defense and Spanish war problems today. The war ministry selected “Big Bill” Gen. Sir Edmund Ironside to head a military court of inquiry to learn who has been “spilling the beans” on secrets of Britain's anti-aircraft defense. Leslie More-Belisha, the dynamic war minister whose combination of boyish enthusiasm and ruthless efficiency has swept him to widespread popularity, stood to play an important role in what the government opposition said might develop into a first class “scandal.” The House of Commons was worked up over the allegation of Duncan Sandys, conservative member of parliament and son-in-law of Winston Churchill, that he was threatened with invocation of the official secrets act—a rigid measure intended to

London, June 28—(AP)—Reliable sources said today that Count Court Haugwitz-Reventlow would come to London to face allegations of his wife, the former Barbara Hutton, that he wrote her letters she considered threatening. It was understood the county's attorney, Norman Brickett, who was counsel for the Duchess of Windsor in her divorce proceedings, would see a Bow Street magistrate tomorrow or Thursday to fix a date for a hearing on the case. Obtains Summons The Woolworth heiress obtained a summons against her husband last week after she received letters which she believed were threatening. Since then her two-year-old son, Lance, has been closely guarded in her Regent’s Park home. The count’s Danish representatives already have indicated he would allow himself to be served with the summons as a prelude to divorce or separation discussions with his American-born wife. LONDON, (AP)—Two British destroyers were ordered suddenly to Mallorca from Gibraltar. The Italian-operated airplane base at Palma, Mallorca, is the source of many of the Insurgent air raids on the coast of Government Spain and British shipping in Spanish waters. Mallorca is 150 miles east of Spain. Observers connected the movement of the destroyers with reports from Rome that Premier Mussolini had interceded with Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco in an effort to halt attacks on British vessels. Both Mussolini's action and the admiralty’s were believed to be results of increasing pressure on Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain at home to do something to stop the attacks. Opposition members of Parliament have been getting more and more sarcastic in asking where the British navy was while ships flying the Union Jack were being sunk.

LONDON, June 29. (UP)—Premier Benito Mussolini has agreed to use his influence to persuade the Spanish nationalists to stop bombing British ships, the foreign office was informed today by Lord Perth, British ambassador to Lord Perth's message to Viscount Halifax, foreign minister, came after he had conferred at length yesterday with Count Ciano, Italian foreign minister, and urged that Italy put pressure on the nationalists. The pressure, according to Italian sources, would be formal and would not involve any admission that Italy controls nationalist Spain. Nevertheless, it was felt here that it would go a long way toward saving the tottering negotiations for a British-Italian agreement. Authoritative sources said Ciano received Lord Perth's representations in the most friendly spirit but contended that the armed forces of nationalist Spain are entirely under the orders of General Franci

Italy interceded, with Spanish Insurgent Generalissimo Francisco Franco today in an effort to get him to halt attacks on British shipping. At almost the same time two British destroyers were ordered from Gibraltar to Mallorca, where the Italians operate an airplane base in the service of the Insurgents. Both Italy's intercession and Britain's movement of the destroyers were believed to be results of increasing pressure on Prime Minister Chamberlain at home to do something to stop attacks on British vessels. Movement “Routine” The Admiralty described the movement of the destroyers as “routine,” but it was believed their trip to Mallorca was a “gesture” to command the Insurgents’ attention and at the same time quiet opposition in parliament. While Britain was stirred by a parliament storm over application of her official secrets act, aimed at espionage, France struck to stamp out increasin

WIMBLEDON, Eng., June 29.--(-- Don Budge, holder of the world’s four major tennis titles, stroked his way into the finals in defense of his British championship today when he defeated Ferenc Puncec of Yugoslavia, 6-2, 6-1, 6-4. The California red-head, who also holds the American, Australian and French titles, will meet England's H. W. (Bunny) Austin in the finals. Austin scored in straight sets today, defeating Henner Henkel of Germany 6-2, 6-4, 6-0. There was no stopping Budge. Puncec was good but it was like Henry Armstrong fighting Joe Louis. When Don went to the net he left poor Puncec helpless and scratching his head. Only in the third set did the red-head let down. Then he stayed on the baseline until Puncec held a 4-2 lead and twice was within a point of a 5-2 advantage. WIMBLEDON, Eng., June 29.—Donald Budge of Oakland, Cal., gained the final round of the All-England singles tennis championships today and will meet Henry W. (Bunny) Austin of England in the title fight. Budge, gangling red-head who is defending champion, moved into the finals with a straight set triumph over Franjo

1938-06-23.text: London, June 22—(4)—A source authorized to speak for the former Barbara Hutton said today she had obtained a court order for possible restraining steps against her titled husband, the 42-year-old Count Court Haugwitz-Reventlow, to safeguard herself and the child. The Danish nobleman was in Paris and there were conflicting reports whether he would come to London today, possibly to shed some light on the mysterious kidnapping and estrangement reports affecting his family. Scotland Yard men were said to be at Croydon airport this morning prepared to serve papers on the count if he returned. One report said he might fly from Paris. The action of the American-born heiress to a five-and-ten store fortune was understood to be based on a dispute with Count Haugwitz-Reventlow over custody of their two-year-old son, Lance, who it has been estimated would inherit $20,000,000 from his mother. A spok

LONDON, June 23 (Thursday) - (P) — The Countess of Strathmore, mother of Queen Elizabeth, died early today at her London home. She was 76 years old. Wife of the Scottish Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne, the Countess had been gravely ill for some time. Both King George VI and the queen were at her bedside when death came.

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, June 22 — The British government calmly ignored the sinking of two more of her merchant ships in the Mediterranean today and continued to canvass the possibilities of a truce in Spain and early operation of her friendship pact with Italy. Prospects of a Spanish armistice appeared to be dimming, but Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain denied in the House of Commons that Italy by current diplomatic negotiations was trying to drive a wedge between Britain and France. There was a brief flurry of optimism after yesterday's agreement by the nonintervention subcommittee on withdrawal of "volunteers" in the Spanish war, an important factor in adjustment of British, French and Italian relations. Britain is pledged to explore the possibilities of truce, but, since Italy is demanding a victory by insurgent Generalissimo Franco and France has agreed to close her fron

LONDON, June 23 (U.P)—Countess Court Haugwitz-Reventlow, the former Barbara Hutton, Woolworth heiress, has started legal proceedings against her husband, it was reported persistently today. The proceedings were apparently in the form of a summons to court and not a warrant of arrest, as reported by the London Evening News and Star. The warrant officer of the Bow Street police court told the United Press that no warrant had been issued “and as far as I know, there are no grounds on which to issue a warrant.” The dispute between the couple was said to be over custody of their two-year-old son, Lance, although Paris reported also that there was disagreement over the investment of Barbara's fortune.

London, June 22 (#).—American-born Countess Barbara Hutton Haugwitz-Reventlow entertained a large house party behind the steel shutters of her massive home tonight after obtaining a secret court order believed intended to protect her baby son, Lance. The surprise court move came along with mounting rumors that she and her Danish nobleman husband, Count Court Haugwitz-Reventlow, were estranged. The Count was conspicuously absent from tonight’s party. The big gates of the Woolworth heiress’ estate in mid-London opened and clicked shut after each guest was allowed to enter. Private guards questioned them carefully and scanned their credentials. The countess, who was said to have received a letter threatening the safety of her baby, disclosed she had taken “certain precautions” to guard him. Chubby, two-year-old Count Lance Haugwitz-Reventlow slept in an air-conditioned, five-room nursery su

London..(4")-King George VI decreed only family mourning for Queen Elizabeth's mother, the 76-year-old Countess of Strathmore and Kinghorne, who died early today. He still had not decided, however, whether to alter plans for a royal visit he and Queen Elizabeth are scheduled to make to Paris next Tuesday. The official announcement that there would be no court mourning for the countess did not mention plans for the sovereigns’ visit abroad. The announcement was made by the Earl of Cromer, the lord chamberlain. Some sources said the death would not affect the royal arrangements but others said the sovereign might go to Paris alone. The countess, wife of the Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne, had been gravely ill of heart trouble for some time. Lord Strathmore, 83, a stately, moustachioed figure, was at his wife's bedside.

NYDE PARK, N. Y., June 22.—(AP)—President Roosevelt dispatched across the Atlantic today a group of nine business, labor, education and government officials to study employer-employee relations in England and Sweden. The group, to which no chairman was named, will report back to the president, through his labor secretary, within a few months on how labor relations are handled in those two countries. Letters of instruction to each of the nine directed them to talk with government, industrial and labor leaders, Mr. Roosevelt commenting that "there is a definite need for an impartial report which will adequately portray the real situation." The president named as follows: Business—Gerard Swope, president of the General Electric Company, New York; Charles R. Hook, president of the American Rolling Mills Company, Middletown, Ohio; Henry F. Harriman, former president of the United States Chamb

LONDON, June 23.--Sir Kingsley Wood, air minister, today announced a drive to increase the strength of the air force personnel by more than 40 per cent. He will seek by March 1939 to recruit more than 2,100 pilots, more than 550 observers, nearly 26,000 tradesmen and unskilled and more than 3,000 boys. The result will be to add more than 30,000 men to the air force which now numbers 72,000. The men to be recruited will equal in number the entire strength of the air force before the expansion program began in 1935. It was explained that the increase was planned in consequence of the production of thousands of war planes and large quantities of equipment and air armament of all kinds.

1938-06-28.text: LONDON —(AP)— The Duchess of Atholl Tuesday gave details of what she said were guns “threatening Gibraltar” from Insurgent Spain and issued notice she would ask Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain in the House of Commons Wednesday what he intends to do about them. The Duchess recently rebelled from conservative ranks and has been a frequent government critic. The question of such guns, allegedly of German manufacture, has been raised repeatedly during the Spanish civil war. The government has taken the position generally that they are not a threat to Gibraltar, Britain’s fortress at the western entrance to the Mediterranean. The Duchess’ question enumerates guns in greater detail than any previous list. It cites more than 20 guns in hills around Insurgent-held Algeciras, including three pieces of more than 10 inches. Mounting indignation over continued bombings of British merchant ships i

' United Press Staff Correspondent London, June 28. (UP)—The British government took issue today with charges by Generalissimo Francisco Franco that British ships are trading with Loyalist Spain in violation of the non-intervention agreement. Franco cited 12 alleged violations. The British government instructed its representative in Nationalist Spain, Sir Robert Hodgson, to inform Franco that Britain and the non-intervention board had investigated the charges and found them without substantiation. In ten cases it was shown definitely that the ships had not violated the agreement, the government said. The eleventh ship, S. S. Marklyn, was trading with the Nationalists and the twelfth ship, the S. S. Orange, was registered as French. All Carried Observers The British government further instructed Hodgson to inform Franco that all British ships mentioned carried non-intervention observers.

New York, June 28.—If the language of diplomacy still retaining any of the strength it possessed in days when knights were bold, then Britain and France have told Japan she is in for trouble should the mikado’s forces carry out their reported project of occupying Hainan island, southernmost port of the Chinese territories. The Anglo-French pair has warned Japan that they will act together in case ‘complications’ arise over Hainan. In these days such a warning may mean much or little, Admittedly it’s not very specific. Still, that is fighting talk and until otherwise convinced we must assume that the allies mean business and are prepared to reach for the guns which each of them is wearing without concealment. Hankow, June 28—The international train draped with American, British, French and German flags departed from Hankow this morning carrying 210 foreigners of seven nationalities, but 26 German advisers to the Chinese army were not aboard. The Germans, it was said, would leave on special coaches to be provided by Chinese authorities on July 5. The international train was routed toward Hongkong. The Berlin government has recalled the German ambassador, Oscar Trautmann, because of apparent displeasure over the reluctance of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek to part with his military experts who are credited with a large share of Chinese war strategy. The German government requested the release of the military mission May 21, and later is reported to have threatened the advisers with loss of citizenship and property confiscation unless they departed. Nineteen years ago today the Versailles treaty was signed, designed to end war, but today the peace of Europe again was menaced by the bombing of British ships in the Spanish Civil War. The British government fought for time, hoping that the situation would solve itself, but it was predicted that a showdown is imminent. Either Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain must take decisive action, meaning belligerent action to protect ships under the British flag, observers said, or the Government must admit that the policy of co-operation with Italy has broken down. Chamberlain's wait-and-see policy may be broken down by the mounting indignation in parliament and among the British public against the apparent desertion of the “Rule Britannia” tradition of the sea. In the wake of yesterday's destruction of two British ships by insurgent bombers came news from Valencia of a new and destructive bombi

WIMBLEDON, England. — American pincers for the "big three" of Helen Wills Moody, Helen Jacobs and Alice Marble in the semifinal round of the all-England tennis championships Tuesday, but the fourth bracket went to towering, angular Mme. Elda Sperling of Germany. Mrs. Moody defeated Kay Stammers, 6-2, 8-1, in the quarter-finals round, with such ease that many of the spectators grew restless and left to watch Miss Marble play Mme. Mathieu. She aced Miss Stammers for the final two match points. Miss Marble won, 6-2, 6-0, profiting by her opponent’s mistakes to gain a 4-1 lead in the first set. Miss Jacobs beat the Polish girl Jadwiga Jedrzejowska, by similar scores, 6-2, 8-4. Seeing the Polish girl forced into one error after another, Miss Jacobs reverted to her old champion, defensive game. A fourth American, Sarah Pate Frey Fabyan, lost to Mme. London, June 22—The startling theory that German aviators attached to Generalissimo Francisco Franco's forces but operating without his foreknowledge have been responsible for recent bombing attacks on British ships in Spanish waters was voiced in diplomatic quarters here today. Usually well-informed sources expressed opinion the object was ‘to sabotage or at least block as long as possible completion of the Anglo-Italian peace agreement as well as to divert British attention from events in central Europe. The belief was predicated on the theory that foreign “volunteers” serving with the Franco side in Spain are able to act more or less autonomously, or in any case to be more responsible to their home governments than to Franco himself. In support of the theory, the informants cited presumably accurate testimony to the effect Franco knew nothing of yesterday's attacks upon the British me

Paris, June 8. (P)X—A source close to the foreign office said tonight that the British-sponsored plan to send a neutral commission into Spain to investigate bombings of civilian centers had struck a snag because Sweden had refused to participate unless the United States did. French diplomatic officials sought to get the Netherlands to take Sweden’s place on the commission, but after a series of conferences reported that no decision had been reached. The United States, invited by Britain to join, rejected the proposal on June 20. Since that time a substitute proposal for a commission composed of British, Swedish and Norwegian members has been under consideration. It had been expected the commission would arrive at Toulouse, France, tonight to begin its work, but the difficulty raised by Sweden probably will delay it until a third neutral can be persuaded to join.

1938-12-03.text: LONDON, Dec. 3 (WP) - Great Britain has asked Italy for an explanation of the anti-French demonstration in the Italian chamber of deputies Wednesday, it was learned from a reliable source today. It was understood that Lord Perth, British ambassador to Rome would see Count Galeazzo Ciano, Italian foreign minister, soon regarding the demonstration.

LONDON, Dec. 2.—(AP)—Men of six nations decided today to tackle Germany again in the international effort to get her estimated 600,000 unwanted Jews out of the country under the $600,000,000 plan sponsored by United States Ambassador Joseph P. Kennedy. The action was taken by the vice-chairmen's committee of the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees, composed of men representing the United States, Great Britain, France, The Netherlands, Brazil and Argentina, the latter a new addition. Previously it was shown Germany had ignored repeated requests that George Rublee, American who is permanent director of the intergovernmental committee, be invited to Berlin to discuss the Jewish emigration problem with German authorities. (By United Press.) London, Dec. 3.—Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain may be forced to cancel his "peace" mission to Italy because of Italian agitation for French possessions, it was reported today. The demands of the Italian press for return of long lost Italian possessions was considered a blow to the Anglo-Italian agreement signed only a fortnight ago and to Chamberlain’s dream of solidifying peace through a program of "appeasement." The agreement was based on a mutual pledge to respect the status quo in the Mediterranean. Any Italian move against Tunis, Nice or Corsica would involve Italy in trouble with Britain as well as France. France moved to line up British support when French Ambassador Charles Corbin acquainted Foreign Secretary Viscount Halifax with latest developments. Corbin told Halifax that Andre Francois-Poncet, new French ambassador to Italy had demanded an explanation

LONDON, Dec. 3 (.R)—New prospects for the settlement of German refugees in French and Dutch colonies and in South American countries have been opened by the six-power refugee committee, it was learned today. The one-day meeting yesterday failed to discover means of giving immediate relief to hard-pressed German Jews but it did carry one stage further a long-range plan to settle thousands of German refugees. Myron C. Taylor of the United States, in outlining the attitude of America, said President Roosevelt believed the solution of the refugee problem would contribute to world appeasement. He described the President's advisory committee for refugees, which he said met weekly to investigate possible places for the settlement of refugees in the United States. London, Eng. (INS) — Fears felt for the safety of Captain E. W. Percival, noted British airplane designer, and three companions, who took off from Heston airport yesterday afternoon for Paris, were dispelled today when they revealed they had landed at the military airport near Versailles. The four had been missing when they failed to arrive on schedule in Paris, where they were to attend an aeronautics demonstration.

Portland, Ore., Dec. 3—(U.P.)—Rain and snow followed a three day ocean storm that raked the Pacific northwest and spread eastward today. The weather bureau forecast diminishing southwestern gales on the Oregon coast as the storm extended inland to Boise, Idaho, and from British Columbia to Redding, California.

Rome, Dec. 3.—(4)—The Fascist campaign for French-controlled territory struck a snag today in France's firm “no.” The French ambassador, André Francois-Poncet, informed Italy that France had no intention of budging from Tunisia—the center of Fascist aspirations—or any other French domains. His formal notice was a protest against a statement by the authoritative Fascist editor, Virginio Gayda, that the Italian nation was “ready to march, even against France, if necessary.” The French ambassador, in a three-quarter hour talk with Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo last night, was understood to have said in more or less direct terms that French withdrawal in the Czechoslovak crisis last September was one thing, but withdrawal from territory ruled by (continued on page ten)

1938-05-28.text: TROON, Scotland —HM— Charley Yates of Atlanta today won the British amateur golf championship, beating Cecil Ewing of Ireland in the 36-hole final, 3 and 2. One up at the end of the morning 18 holes, in which each shot a four-over-par 75, Yates shot even par for the 16 holes of the afternoon round. He was three up at 27, lost the 28th as he got into trouble the only time on the round, then finished with five pars and a birdie. At the final hole Charley hit a fine mashie niblick shot, to within eight feet of the cup while the giant Irishman was in a trap to the left of the green in three. Ewing marched into the sand, exploded out nine feet away and knocked the putt into the back of the cup. Then Yates, without hesitation, stroked his ball home to win.

TROON, Scotland, May 28. — Charley Yates of Atlanta, Ga., regained his form after a shaky start and won the British amateur golf championship with a victory over Cecil Ewing, Irish Walker Cup star, in the thirty-six hole final today. Yates was the first American to win the title since Lawson Little turned the trick for the second successive year in 1935. Yates won by 3 and 2. Yates trailed the Irish insurance agent from County Sligo throughout most of the morning round. Twice during this round Ewing was two up. Yates’ play was uncertain and he was exceedingly nervous. But when he leveled the match on the sixteenth green he relaxed and returned to the form which had carried him to the final.

DUBLIN, May 28.—(U.P)—Prime Minister DeValera dissolved the Lower House of Parliament (Dail Eireann) today and called for a general election June 17 because of a one-vote parliamentary defeat, his first since 1932. DeValera announced that he would start the election campaign, the first since the free state became Eire or Ireland, in Monaghan county tomorrow. The House Wednesday night defeated the government 51 to 50 by adopting a motion of William T. Cosgrave, leader of the United Ireland party, to establish an arbitration board to which civil servants might submit grievances. Standing of parties in the lower house was: DeValera’s Fianna Fail party, 67 seats; United Ireland, 48; Labor 13 and Independents 8. Thus the combined opposition could defeat DeValera at any time.

Madrid, May 28—A bomb fell into the hold of the British ship Great End during the bombing of Valencia today and the ship, badly damaged, began sinking slowly. The Great End was badly damaged by bombs on May 14th.

Hendaye, France, (At the Spanish Frontier), May 28. UP—Insurgent dispatches today told of an entire government division being shot to pieces in a futile attempt to storm the defenses of Tremp, a vital hydroelectric power center on the Catalonian front. In this sector the government for days has been struggling to recover some of the ground lost when insurgents hammered up to the Catalonian border in their great drive earlier in the spring. Insurgents said the government division attacked the San Cornelio range, forming the eastern defenses of Tremp, and that only one company was able to regain government lines after the assault failed. Advices reaching the border said the government had massed more than 35,000 men along the 10-mile sector just east of Tremp.

(By the Associated Press) BERLIN, May 27—As if by order, the German press today ceased blasts against Czechoslovakia and western democracies it accused of pro-Czechoslovak sympathies. The will in war-like talk was said in official quarters to be due to Adolf Hitler's determination to preserve peace in spite of "provocations" by Czechoslovaks. Provocations Cited Among "provocations" were the defense preparations of last week and alleged border violations by military airplanes. The only new incident reported today was in Kaplice (Kaplitzy, north of Linz), where an Austrian German farmer allegedly was ill-treated by Czechoslovak soldiers because he could not produce his identity card. Troops Withdrawn In connection with the sudden quiet, it was stated here that "not only have no German troops been dispatched to the frontier but two whole regiments sent into Austria at the time of Anschluss

BARCELONA, May 28 (4) - Eight low-flying planes bombed Barcelona heavily this morning. The raiders were clearly visible in the blue sky as they roared through a terrific blaze of anti-aircraft fire. The bombardment lasted 50 minutes and was concentrated in the southern part of the port city. Immediate reports on casualties and damage were not available. Nine tri-motored insurgent bombers also raided Valencia but no casualties or damage were reported. Spanish government officials said Major Julian Troncoso, former insurgent military governor of Lérida who spent seven months in a French jail for complicity in an attempt to seize the Spanish government submarine C2 at Brest, France, had been killed when government forces captured Baltus, on a front in western Catalonia.

Berlin, May 28—Charges that German war planes had illegally crossed the Czech border were made by the Czechoslovakian minister today in a formal protest to the Nazi government. On several occasions, the protest said, the German planes flew as far into Czechoslovakia as Pilsen, where the gigantic Skoda munitions works are located. The German government has twice protested similar border violations by Czech planes. (EDITOR'S NOTE: How the

1938-06-01.text: Epsom, Eng., June 1—Bois Roussel, French-bred horse owned by P. Beatty, today won the 159th derby before the King and Queen and some 400,000 of their subjects.

BARCELONA, May 31.—(AP)— A swift and terrible foray by a squadron of tri-motored Insurgent bombers took a heavy toll of dead and injured today in the crowded Catalan town of Granollers, 16 miles north of Barcelona. Estimates of the dead ran as high as 500. There were many wounded. British Freighter Sunk Almost simultaneously the British freighter Penthames was bombed and sunk in an Insurgent air raid on Valencia harbor and inmates of three Madrid hospitals were endangered in an intensive Insurgent shelling of the southwestern part of that city. Five tri-motored Insurgent planes poured a torrent of bombs on the Granollers market place and on long lines of men, women and children waiting to get potato rations. The raid caught many women out for morning marketing. At one spot 50 persons were killed, at another, 55. Some 25 buildings were destroyed. Hospital facilities in the town, whose nor

NEW YORK, June 1.—(#)—Twenty-three Irish Hospitals sweepstakes tickets held in the United States won $1,925,000 on the running of the English derby at Epsom Downs today. This hiked the total winnings in the United States on the rare and previous drawings from the sweepstakes drum to $3,920,980. Americans had paid about $46,800,000 for their hopes for sudden wealth. Each of five of the 28 tickets on winning horses paid their owners $150,000 when Bois Roussel came in first. Scottish Union, second, won $75. (Concluded on Page 7)

EPSOM, England, June 1, CUP)—Peter Beatty's Bois Roussel today won the 158th running of the Epsom Derby, bringing a fortune of some $50,000 to its owner and determining the distribution of millions of dollars in sweepstakes prizes all over the world. King George, Queen Elizabeth and Queen Mary accompanied by other members of the royal family, saw the race from the royal box while hundreds of thousands of their subjects looked on from the grandstand, from bus tops and along the railing. Estimates of the crowd varied from 500,000 to 1,000,000 persons. Heavy rain fell throughout the race.

LONDON, June 1. —(#)— Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain told the House of Commons today that Great Britain is still fully resolved to accept the obligation entered into on signing the Kellogg-Briand pact. Chamberlain's statement was an expression of agreement with the declaration of Cordell Hull, United States Secretary of State, who on May 28 reminded the powers that they had given their solemn word to refrain from war in signing the Kellogg-Briand pact in 1928.

Associated Press Foreign Writer NEW YORK, June 1—Speaking of bombing defenseless civilians: One day back in 1917 a German army flyer—a captain chap—came winging low over a French village in the British war-zone. Beneath him (among other things, be it noted) was one of the largest of the English army base-hospitals, as was blazoned to the sky in the huge red crosses on the roofs of the long rows of squat buildings. A bright sun threw these symbols of mercy into bold relief. Suddenly a bomb came screaming out of the blue—and exploded in the hospital grounds. Several nurses were injured, and many lives were endangered. British machine-guns began to chatter, for the enemy plane was circling daringly within their range. And the raiding captain paid for his boldness when he came hurtling to earth—inside the hospital zone, too. Still he experienced a miracle and his only hurt, barring his pride

LONDON, June 1—(P)— Prime Minister Chamberlain told the House of Commons today that the government had a compulsory military service bill ready for submission to Parliament in the event of war. He added, however, that the bill, in preparation since 1922, did not provide for general conscription of manpower or application of the compulsory service principle to industry. Chamberlain made his statement in an effort to quell a two-day furor over conscription, arising from much-debated remarks Monday by Sir Thomas Inskip, minister for co-ordination of defense. Earlier Chamberlain had told the House that Britain still is “fully resolved to accept the obligation” entered into when she signed the Kellogg-Briand pact 10 years ago. 1 C-1058, by International News Service, WASHINGTON, June 1. —The United States has been apprised unofficially of a proposal by British interests to exchange American airplanes for British ocean vessels, it was revealed today. At the same time, it was learned that the British aviation mission, which recently concluded a visit to this country and Canada, will recommend purchase of a large number of American military aircraft. According to British embassy attachés, the British government probably would look with favor on the proposal to swap ocean vessels for airplanes. Although this suggestion was advanced in England prior to the aviation mission's departure for the United States, it was not laid formally before the American government.
